It is any datatrove DataFolder (a local folder, S3, any fsspec path) that every worker can reach: no server, no lock service, no queue. Workers write small JSON files, list the folder and read the modification times the storage reports. The code is linecaster.net.broker; proxies are the first kind of resource it coordinates (linecaster.net.proxies).

Terms are the glossary's: broker, lease, mark, worker identity (worker slot).

items.title: Why
items.text: A worker that keeps something to itself (a rate limiter, a list of blocked proxies) is right only if no other worker uses the same thing. Servers count requests per IP, so per proxy, and block per IP; a run has many workers (local processes, Ray tasks, HF Jobs) on several machines, and several runs may use the same proxies. The broker gives each proxy one owner at a time, so what the owner enforces for it holds for everyone, and makes a block that one worker found visible to whoever uses that proxy next.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
<broker>/
  broker.json                          {"format": "linecaster.broker/1", "created": ...}
  workers/<worker>.json                heartbeat: machine, slot, run, started, renewed
  slots/<machine>/<n>/leases/...       the worker slots of a machine
  <kind>/<resource id>/
    leases/<claimed>-<worker>.json     who holds it, since when
    marks/<scope>/<until>-<n>.json     what holds for it until when

The layout is versioned (broker.json's format) and neutral: a kind of resource is a folder name and its resources are ids, so a new kind needs no change of the protocol. File names are deterministic (times, worker ids, counters; no random parts).

Kind Resource id Leases Marks slots <machine>/<n> the process that is worker <machine>-<n> now none proxies a hash of the proxy's host and port (linecaster.net.proxies.proxy_id); no credential reaches the folder the worker that sends requests through the proxy a block at a host (scope: the host, until the block ends); a broken proxy (scope *, every host)

items.title: Protocol
items.text:
Liveness. A lease or a heartbeat is valid while its file was written within the lease time (LEASE_TTL, 180 s), by the modification time the storage lists. A worker renews every 60 s (RENEW_SECONDS): it rewrites its lease files and its heartbeat. A worker that crashes stops renewing, and its leases expire on their own. The age of a file is the reader's clock against the storage's, so the writers' clocks do not matter, and machines whose clocks are kept by NTP agree.

Claims. There is no exclusive create on object storage, so a claim is decided by listing:

  1. list the resource's leases/; if another worker's lease is valid, the claim fails (expired leases found on the way are deleted);
  2. write the own lease, <claimed>-<worker>.json, the claim's time in its name;
  3. list again: the earliest valid lease wins, by the time in its name, then by the worker id; a loser deletes its own lease.

Two workers that claim at once mostly both see both leases in step 3 and agree on the winner. When one listed before the other's write had landed (object storage takes a moment), both may believe they won; the next renew settles it: the holder whose lease is not the earliest valid one gives the resource up and logs at INFO worker X lost a claim race for proxies/<id> to Y; it takes another (a proxy pool then claims a replacement at once). A holder's lease keeps its claim time across renews, so it stays the earliest. A holder that went without a renew for longer than the lease time (a stalled process) finds at its next renew that its lease file is gone (deleted as expired by another worker) or older than the lease time; it gives the resource up and logs a WARNING, lease on proxies/<id> expired (no renew within the lease time).

Marks. A mark holds for a resource in a scope (a host, or * for every scope) for ttl seconds from its file's modification time. It is written once and never changed; whoever sees it expired deletes it, past its keep seconds if it has them: a mark with keep stays readable that long after its end, no longer holding, so its data (a proxy's doubling, last_wait) reaches whoever claims the resource next (linecaster.net.broker.Resource.last). A reader reads a mark's file once (it never changes) and keeps its end. The record is JSON: ttl, until (the end on the writer's clock, informational), worker, and the kind's data (status, last_wait, keep for proxies). A reader ignores the fields it does not know: a broker that does not know keep deletes a kept mark at its end (the doubling then starts again), and a mark without keep and last_wait is deleted at its end and starts the doubling at 60 s.

Fair share. Sharing them fairly (proxies with per_worker: share, the default), a worker holds ceil(free / live workers) resources of a kind (at least one if any is free), where the live workers are the valid heartbeats. Proxies count as free for a host when no mark blocks them there.

Worker identity. A worker is a datatrove worker slot of its machine, <machine>-<n>, not a process: on Ray every task is a new process, and the harvest runs one item per task, so leases tied to processes would change hands every few seconds. At its first use a process claims a free slot of its machine (slots/<machine>/<n>, a lease held by the process itself) and is that worker from then on. Its search starts at a slot of its own, so processes started together do not race for the same slots: the executor's worker index (linecaster.net.broker.set_worker_index: datatrove's local rank in a local run's pool, the rank modulo the tasks at once on Ray, the task's GPU in a multi-GPU Job), else a random place. From one listing of the machine's slots and one of the heartbeats it takes a handed-over slot first (a live heartbeat whose slot no process holds: its leases wait for a successor), then, with worker index k, the k-th free slot, then the free slots upward from there, past every valid lease. Free counts the slots not held since before this launch: those without a valid slot lease claimed more than a minute ago (SLOT_PEERS_SECONDS; a lease keeps its claim time across renews). The slots of a run stopped moments ago, whose leases are still valid, are left out of the count, so a relaunch takes the slots past them at one claim per process instead of racing upward through them; the slots its peers claimed meanwhile are not, so a pool whose processes look one after the other still takes slots 0 to n−1. Processes started together with distinct worker indexes need one claim each (tests/test_broker.py). A process that ends hands its slot over (Broker.hand_over: the slot's lease is deleted, the worker's other leases stay), and the next process on that machine claims that slot (handed-over slots come first), is the same worker, finds the worker's leases (named after it) and renews them. On Ray each task hands over at its end (linecaster.execution.ray.RayExecutor); a local run's worker processes outlive their tasks and keep their slots, and a process that ends normally hands over at its exit. A slot whose process crashed expires like any lease, and so do the leases of a slot no process takes over.

items.title: Proxies
items.text:
A worker's proxy pool (linecaster.net.proxies.ProxyPool, used by linecaster.net.http.HTTPFetcher when a proxy list is set) works on the broker:

  • A fair share per worker (the default; an HTTP policy's proxies: {per_worker: share}). The worker claims at most 2 when it looks for proxies (FIRST_FILL) and grows toward its fair share of the proxies not blocked for its hosts at each check of its pool (every 10 s in use, REBALANCE_SECONDS, and after each renew; at most doubling each time), where it also gives back the ones beyond its share, those blocked for its hosts first. A worker that joins gets its part within seconds, one that leaves frees its part within the lease time, and the first workers of a launch do not take the proxies of those still starting. A few workers then use every proxy, which suits a run whose limit is not the proxies, such as one writing to object storage.
  • One proxy per worker (proxies: {per_worker: 1}). The worker claims one free proxy usable for the host it fetches, in an order of its own (so workers claiming at once try different proxies first), and sends every request through it. When the proxy is blocked or broken (below), the worker marks it, releases it and claims another free usable one at once. No fair share and no rebalancing: the host's rate limits per proxy are the worker's own. With several hosts, a worker whose proxy is blocked at one of them keeps it for the others and swaps it for a free proxy usable at every host it uses, if there is one. Using every proxy takes as many workers as proxies, which suits output on local disk or a short proxy list.
  • Up to N per worker (proxies: {per_worker: N}). As with one, the proxies claimed one by one: one when the worker holds none usable, then one more at each check of its pool, up to N and never more (more inherited from its slot's earlier process are given back).
  • Rate limits per proxy. With a proxy list the host's rate limits hold per proxy (per IP). The owner spaces the requests through a proxy to a host by the strictest limit and sends each request through the owned proxy whose turn comes first. One owner per proxy makes the limit hold across all workers and runs that share the broker. When a proxy changes hands (a worker gives it back for the fair share, swaps it or releases it), the owner first marks its next free turn at each host (scope turn-<host>, ending at that turn) and the next owner starts there no earlier, so the old owner's requests already on their way and the new owner's first ones keep the spacing too. These marks are not blocks: the status and the count of available proxies leave them out.
  • Blocks. A status in the host's block_on (429 by default) and, with html there, an HTML page where another format was expected mark the proxy for that host (http): until the response's Retry-After, else for 60 s, twice the last wait on each repeat of that proxy at that host, at most the host's block_ttl (an hour by default). The mark records the status (429, html) and the doubling below. The owner stops using it there at once, and releases it once it is blocked for every host it uses; a worker that claims it later reads the mark with the claim, so no worker sends requests into another's block and starts the server's block window again. The request goes on through another proxy without counting as an attempt.
  • Broken proxies. A proxy error or no connection to the proxy, broken_after times in a row (3 by default), marks it for every host (*, status broken): first for broken_ttl (300 s), twice as long each time it breaks again before it carries an answer, at most block_ttl. Its doubling travels with the proxy as a block's does.
  • The doubling travels with the proxy. Each block or broken mark without Retry-After records its wait (last_wait; a mark with Retry-After the doubling's last wait unchanged) and is kept that long past its end (keep), so a worker that claims a released proxy continues the doubling where its last owner left it (60, 120, 240 s across workers) instead of starting at 60 s. While a worker holds a proxy it is the only one using it, so it keeps the doubling in memory from its claim on (and writes it into each mark). The doubling starts again at 60 s: after a successful response through the proxy from that host (any answer through it, for a broken proxy's), in that worker at once and for everyone else by deleting the proxy's ended marks there (in a thread; until then, or if that fails, the next owner doubles once more than it should, never less); or after a quiet period, when the next block comes more than its last wait after the last block there ended (linecaster.net.http.doubling; the kept mark is gone by then). An answer to a request sent before a block that still holds changes nothing. The rule is the direct path's too, where a worker keeps each host's doubling in memory. Why these two: a successful response is the only sure sign the host lets the IP in again, and the quiet period bounds how long a mark is kept, as long as the block before it, so a proxy that nobody tried for that long is not punished for an old episode.
  • No proxy usable. When every proxy the worker holds is blocked for a host and none is free to claim, the worker's requests to that host pause until a block it knows of ends or another worker gives a proxy back (it looks again at once when a block ends, else every 5 s, FILL_SECONDS) (one warning at the start, one at the end; the time is in the fetch records' pause_seconds). Once these waits since the host's last successful response would pass its max_pause (http), the run stops (StopRequests).

--broker PATH (or an HTTP policy's root key broker) names the folder; the default is OUT/logs/broker. Runs pointed at one path share the proxies and their blocks. A run's default worker count comes from the broker too (linecaster.execution.run.allocate): from the proxies available at launch (the proxies in the file, less those with a live block or broken mark for the run's hosts and those leased by live workers of other runs, read with linecaster.net.broker.survey_kind), one per available proxy and at most one per CPU sharing them fairly, divided by N with per_worker 1 or N, and at most 64 with OUT on object storage (pipelines); on local and Ray runs only (on HF Jobs each worker is a Job, so a proxy list never sets their number).

items.title: The command
items.text:
linecaster broker reads and tidies a broker's folder (PATH: any fsspec path, e.g. OUT/logs/broker or s3://bucket/broker). The code is linecaster.net.broker.survey_all, clean and purge, usable from code with a now to judge liveness by.

Command Does linecaster broker status PATH [--json] from one listing: the format; the workers (machine, run, time since the last renew), live and stale; the worker slots per machine; per kind of resource how many there are, held by a live lease, held only by expired ones (stale), free, blocked per scope with the latest end, broken (*), and the expired marks. Ids only, no credential (proxies are hashes). --json: one JSON object with the same content linecaster broker clean PATH removes what has expired: heartbeats and leases (slots and resources) not renewed within the lease time, marks past their end and their keep (a kept mark holds a proxy's doubling). Safe while a run uses the broker linecaster broker clean PATH --leases also every heartbeat, slot lease and resource lease, live or not; the marks (blocks) stay linecaster broker clean PATH --marks also every mark, live, kept or not: blocked and broken proxies are tried again at once, and their doubling starts again at 60 s linecaster broker purge PATH resets the broker: removes every file of its layout, broker.json among them, so the next run starts as on an empty folder

clean and purge take --dry-run (list what would be removed, remove nothing) and -v (list each removed file); clean prints the counts per category otherwise. Confirmation: clean --leases or --marks that would remove something live (renewed within the lease time, a mark not expired), and purge always, list what they would remove and ask on a terminal; without one they refuse. --yes skips the question. Both refuse a folder that is not a broker's (clean: no broker.json of this format; purge: neither broker.json nor workers/ or slots/), and neither removes a file outside the broker's layout. Exit codes: 0 done (or nothing to do), 1 refused or aborted, 2 a usage error.

After a hard kill (kill -9, a crash, a local run whose worker processes are terminated) nothing hands over: the dead workers' heartbeats, slots and proxy leases look valid for up to the lease time (3 min). A run started again within that time gets new slot numbers, finds every proxy held and pauses until the leases expire. Once no process of the killed run is left, linecaster broker clean PATH --leases removes them, and the next run gets the slots of its worker indexes and claims the proxies at once; the blocks found before stay, so no worker sends requests into a block again. Add --marks only when the blocks themselves are wrong (a fixed proxy list, a host that lifted its block).

Which to use: plain clean any time, also as a cron job beside running workers (it only deletes what a worker would delete when it sees it); clean --leases after a hard kill; clean --leases --marks to start the proxies afresh while keeping the folder; purge to reset a broker completely (a test folder, a broker of an older format, a folder to hand over empty). clean --leases --marks and purge remove the same live files; purge also removes broker.json and the folders left empty.

items.title: Guarantees and limits
items.text:
• One owner per resource, as long as workers renew within the lease time. A worker stalled for longer than that (a frozen process, a storage outage) can briefly share a resource with the worker that claimed it meanwhile, until one of them renews and gives it up (at most a renew interval).
  • Per-proxy limits hold across workers, since only the owner sends requests through a proxy and it enforces the limits locally.
  • Liveness comes from storage modification times, compared with the reader's clock. The storage must list modification times (local folders and object stores do); a mark without one falls back to the end written in it.
  • Costs are listings and small writes: a renew rewrites the worker's leases and heartbeat and lists each kind it holds once a minute; a worker that looks for proxies lists the kind at most every 5 s (FILL_SECONDS), at once after it gave one up. Claims of many workers at once are spread by trying the free resources in an order of each worker's own, and slot claims by starting at each process's worker index.
  • What the broker does not do: no queue, no ordering of work, no exclusive create, no consistency stronger than the storage's own listings. Hugging Face buckets are not checked for the listing consistency the claims rely on.

items.title: Future kinds (not implemented)
items.text:
The same protocol fits other shared resources; these are examples, none of them exists:

  • direct/<machine>: a machine's own IP as a resource with its own rate limits and blocks, for direct connections.
  • servers/<endpoint>: a model server's capacity, leased by the workers that send it requests.
  • quotas/<host>: a host's request budget for a day, divided among workers.
  • items/<item id>: an item's work claimed by one worker at a time.

items.title: The catalog: models, presets, recipes, policies, conventions, normalizations, strategies, vocabularies
items.text:
The catalog describes every model Linecaster can run, how it runs it, and the tested combinations. Its entries live in one folder, src/linecaster/catalog/data/, shipped with linecaster; linecaster.catalog reads, validates and resolves them.

src/linecaster/catalog/data/
  models/<id>/model.yaml, model.md        # + upstream/<revision>/ (the upstream card, verbatim)
  presets/<step>/<id>.yaml, <id>.md       # one folder per step (STEPS)
  recipes/<id>.yaml, <id>.md
  policies/<id>.yaml
  conventions/<format>/<id>.yaml, <id>.md # one folder per format; the prose is required
  normalizations/<id>.yaml                # one rule each
  strategies/<id>.yaml                    # named lists of normalizations
  vocabularies/<scheme>.yaml              # what a classification scheme's values mean
  catalog.index                           # generated: every entry's hash
src/linecaster/catalog/schemas/<kind>.json        # generated from the Pydantic models

items.title: What the catalog holds
items.text:
The catalog and its docs are organized by ten kinds: engines and pipelines (code, by versioned id) and eight kinds of catalog entry (models, presets, recipes, policies, conventions, normalizations, strategies, vocabularies; a YAML file each). The kinds of entry are one table in the code (linecaster.catalog.registry.KINDS: each kind's files, format, id rule, index table and prose rule), so loading, the index and the checks of prose are the same for all.

Kind Is Named Lives in engine code that implements one step: runs a model, or applies rules versioned id: kraken.recognition.v1, hierarchy.ratios.v1 engines/<engine>/ (a package each); chat.v1 and the rule-based engines in linecaster (linecaster.engines) model one upstream artifact at pinned revisions, with its card slug: kraken-ppocrv6-medium models/<id>/model.yaml preset an engine, a model pin and the engine's options, ready to use slug: kraken-ppocrv6-medium presets/<step>/<id>.yaml pipeline code: a template with slots and the run-anywhere command line versioned id: transcribe_modular.v1 (the script's name) pipelines/<name>.py recipe a named combination: a pipeline, a preset per slot, options slug: squiddle recipes/<id>.yaml policy a rendering policy: which annotations go into which layer of a rendering, and whose count where several annotators gave one slug: page-layers policies/<id>.yaml conventions what one public source's markup means: rules an importer applies, each a match and a decision; may extend one other entry slug: enwikisource conventions/<format>/<id>.yaml normalization one named change of a text, applied when a text is written, never stored slug: long-s normalizations/<id>.yaml strategy a transcription strategy: normalizations in order, to write texts or to compare them (a lane) slug: latin-historic, alnum strategies/<id>.yaml vocabulary what the values of one classification scheme mean: each value's definition, what counts and what does not the scheme: role, degraded vocabularies/<scheme>.yaml

Besides these: the index (catalog.index: every entry's hash) and the run record (OUT/run.yaml, and per page each Annotator of the page record: what a run resolved).

items.title: Ids and versions
items.text:
Term Whose Meaning Example version upstream what upstream calls it, verbatim, never parsed PP-OCRv6 medium, Chandra 2 revision upstream the exact identity of the files HF commit, version DOI, git commit, sha256 .v<n> linecaster the contract of an engine's options or a pipeline's slots and options transcribe_modular.v1 schema linecaster the format of a YAML file linecaster.preset release linecaster the package version: it versions the catalog's entries too (release versioning) 0.10.0
  • Slugs (models, presets, recipes, policies): lowercase [a-z0-9.-]. They may contain upstream names (deepseek-ocr-2), never our versions. Ids are unique across presets and recipes, so a name means one thing.
  • Code ids (CODE_ID): lowercase dotted names ending in .v<n>. An incompatible change is a new id (.v2); the old one stays registered. Adding an option is compatible when its default keeps the old behavior; changing a default, removing or renaming an option is not.
  • A reference is an entry's id. What it does is identified by the hash of its functional content (the index; run records store it with the entry's settings). A reference from before 0.10, id@edition, resolves to this release's entry with an EditionWarning (linecaster.catalog.registry.split_ref).
  • A tag or branch is resolved to a commit when a model is pinned; the tag is kept as tag: for information. Zenodo: the version DOI identifies the files, the concept DOI is information. Downloads without a commit: the file's sha256 is the revision.

items.title: Files
items.text:
A catalog entry is a YAML file, the data, validated strictly by linecaster.catalog.schema (unknown keys are errors), and a Markdown file of the same name next to it, the prose for people (why these settings, limitations, changes), without front matter. Tools read only the YAML; the docs generator also includes the prose. The prose is optional, except for presets and recipes with support: core and conventions. The index is YAML only, and so is an evidence record (kept outside the catalog, below). Bulk data (page records, exports) is JSON Lines or Parquet, not catalog data.

Format Schema id JSON Schema model linecaster.model schemas/model.json preset linecaster.preset schemas/preset.json recipe linecaster.recipe schemas/recipe.json policy linecaster.policy schemas/policy.json conventions linecaster.conventions schemas/conventions.json normalization linecaster.normalization schemas/normalization.json strategy linecaster.strategy schemas/strategy.json vocabulary linecaster.vocabulary schemas/vocabulary.json evidence (not catalog data; its schema ships here) linecaster.evidence/3 (/2 and /1 are read too) schemas/evidence-3.json, -2, -1 benchmark (not catalog data) linecaster.benchmark/2 (/1 is read, upgraded) schemas/benchmark-2.json run record (OUT/run.yaml, not catalog data) linecaster.run-record/2 schemas/run-record-2.json page record, document (data, not catalog data) linecaster.page/6, linecaster.document/2 schemas/page-6.json, schemas/document-2.json

Catalog entries carry no version in their schema id: the release versions them. The data formats keep their own versions (compatibility).

Every YAML file names its format twice: its first line is # yaml-language-server: $schema=<relative path to src/linecaster/catalog/schemas/<kind>.json> (for editors), and its field schema holds the schema id (for tools). The JSON Schemas are generated from the Pydantic models (linecaster catalog schemas); the test suite fails when a committed one differs from a fresh one.

YAML has 1.2 semantics, read with ruamel.yaml through linecaster.catalog.yamlio: only true / false are booleans (NO stays Norwegian), and a duplicate key is an error. Values that look like numbers or versions are quoted ("1.0"). Commands that write a file back (pin) keep its comments.

items.title: Model (models/<id>/model.yaml)
items.text:
Field Meaning id, version our slug; upstream's name, verbatim source kind (hf, zenodo, git, url) and ref (repo id, concept DOI, repository URL, download URL) pins one entry per upstream revision: revision, tag, doi, pinned (date), files (name → sha256:<hex>), card, card_sha256, license_file license SPDX id where there is one, else the license's own name languages, scripts ISO 639-3 (mul for many), ISO 15924 params parameter count, as upstream states it derived_from ref and relation (mirror, converted, quantized, finetuned)

The upstream card is always copied, verbatim, at the pinned revision, whatever its license: Hugging Face README.md, the HTRMoPo record, a repository README; a separate license file next to it. Its sha256 is in the pin. Cards are never edited; license, languages and scripts in model.yaml are taken from them where they say. A new upstream revision is a new entry in pins, with its own upstream/<revision>/ folder. Model entries are written by linecaster catalog pin.

items.title: Preset (presets/<step>/<id>.yaml)
items.text: Field Meaning id, step the step must match the folder model id and revision of a model pin submodels further pins of a multi-model engine, by role engine the engine's id: engine: kraken.recognition.v1 options the engine's options (its Options model) settings prompts, sampling and other request settings (chat presets; repair: the repair pass's max_tokens, 0 for off, and temperature) labels native layout label → region label, from which the layout step classifies each region's content role (the native label stays the region's label); unmapped labels are text by_script a by-script engine's strategies: ISO 15924 script code → preset id of the same step, and "*" → the default for every other script (required) serve the server it runs on: server (vllm, sglang, linecaster, vendor), version (vLLM: linecaster's, VLLM_VERSION, 0.30.0, unless the preset names another), image (for HF Jobs; vLLM: that release's vllm/vllm-openai image unless named), flags, env, revision_flag, pin_ignore, server_packages, draft (speculative decoding); a vendor's service also command, health, weights_dir (page engines) capabilities unit (line, region, page, item) and produces (the parts it adds, vocabulary PARTS) provenance derived_from (sources of the settings, each at a commit or revision), authored_by, created support, superseded_by see Support

items.title: Recipe (recipes/<id>.yaml)
items.text:
Field Meaning id pipeline the pipeline it fills: pipeline: transcribe_modular.v1 presets slot → preset id options the pipeline's options, by name (squiddle's text: the item texts it writes, <strategy>:<format>) provenance, support, superseded_by as for presets

A recipe's environment and entry point is its script recipes/<id>.py (see Pipelines, recipes and launch.py); a recipe a downstream project runs lives in this catalog too (squiddle).

items.title: Policy (policies/<id>.yaml)
items.text:
Field Meaning id description what the policy is for (prose, not part of its functional content) rules the rules, the first that matches wins: role, production, status, motivation (each left out: any) and to, the layer (body, furniture, background, invisible, notes, metadata, none); without a match, the role's default layer precedence per scheme (role, heading_level, ...) or order: the steps or annotator names whose annotations count first; the latest annotator otherwise tables, markdown what counts as a table when written out; the Markdown a rendering writes

A policy entry is a linecaster.data.policy.RenderingPolicy with a schema and a description (PolicyDoc); the data model says what it decides. The catalog ships page-layers, the policy a component renders with unless it is given another (DEFAULT_POLICY_REF; in code without the catalog, linecaster.data.DEFAULT_POLICY), and page-layers-described, the same with descriptions in the body. Components and pipelines name a policy by id (--policy); linecaster.catalog.registry.rendering_policy resolves it. A policy decides layers, never text: what a text is written as is its strategy's.

items.title: Normalization (normalizations/<id>.yaml)
items.text:
One concern, one rule (linecaster.normalization.rules for the rules on characters, linecaster.document.strategy for those on a document's structure). A normalization is applied when a text is written or compared, never stored in a record.

Field Meaning id, description scripts, languages the ISO 15924 scripts it is meant for (* any); BCP 47 tags (a language-specific one is never in a default) use output (a text written), comparison (a lane), or both subsumes normalizations whose effect this one includes (nfkc: nfc, long-s, ligatures), for the conventions check of scoring rule exactly one: on characters unicode (NFC, NFKC), map (a table; the longest key first), patterns (regular expressions in order, each a match, its flags (I, M, S), a replace (a space by default) and an engine: Python's re, the default, or regex, the regex package, for Unicode properties such as \p{Ll}), case (fold, lower), keep (only these characters), whitespace (collapse), latex (text: each LaTeX formula as the characters it prints); on the document edits (the source's corrections, expansions, regularizations applied), divided_words: source (a word the source marks as divided written whole), division_marks: unicode-marks (squiddleocr's rule, the document's words as its lexicon), flow (the rows of a component joined: by a space, or none where Unicode's line breaking joins the words; a row ending in an unresolved division mark joined without a space, the mark kept)

The catalog ships the normalizations of the strategies below and of the lanes: nfc, nfkc, long-s, ligatures, r-rotunda, superscript-e, quotes, dashes, invisible, whitespace, casefold, lowercase, latex-text, markup, html-tags, letters-digits, letters-marks-digits, ascii-letters-digits, editors-corrections, editors-expansions, editors-regularizations, divided-words, unicode-marks, flow, and for other writing traditions arabic-tatweel, arabic-marks, arabic-letters, persian-arabic-letters (Persian and Urdu), hebrew-points, greek-monotonic, cyrillic-prereform (Russian), japanese-iteration-marks and romanian-comma-below (Romanian). For comparing international typography (Omni Parse Bench's comparison fold, Apache-2.0) it ships hierarchy (quotes, primes, the minus sign and other dash-likes, spaces, arrows, the fraction slash, the ellipsis, a decimal middle dot), cjk-punctuation (CJK and full-width punctuation as ASCII), checkboxes (as ☒ and ☐), footnote-markers ([1], [^a] as their label), bullets (a bullet glyph starting a line), leaders (runs of dots, dashes, underscores), superscript-digits (set apart after a digit) and line-end-hyphens (a hyphen at a line's end joined before a lowercase letter: dehyphenation, which no shipped strategy names). None is applied unless a strategy names it: dividing words, dehyphenating, modernizing letter forms are a strategy's choice, never a default.

items.title: Strategy (strategies/<id>.yaml)
items.text:
Field Meaning id, description literal is built in (no normalization: the text as read) and is no file use output (a text written: --text latin-historic:md) or comparison (a scoring lane) normalizations the normalizations by id, in the order they apply

Catalog.strategy(ref) resolves literal, a strategy's id, or an unnamed strategy: normalizations and strategies joined by + (latin-historic+unicode-marks+flow), each strategy its normalizations. The catalog ships latin-historic (nfc, long-s, ligatures, r-rotunda, superscript-e) for output and the lanes diplomatic, reading, typographic, alnum, alnum-nonmark and ascii-alnum for comparison, diplomatic the default lane (evaluation).

items.title: Vocabulary (vocabularies/<scheme>.yaml)
items.text:
Field Meaning scheme the classification scheme it defines (linecaster.data.SCHEMES), also its id and file name description what the scheme classifies, in a sentence targets what it classifies, narrowest first: span, word, line, region, page values the closed list of values, each a definition (one or two sentences that stand on their own), counts (cases that are this value) and does_not_count (cases that are not, naming what they are instead where one can) open, pattern an open scheme (language, script) lists no values; its values match pattern answers a property scheme's (values yes and no): the answer that means each, named after the property (yes: degraded, no: not_degraded), so that a model's "yes" cannot be read as "yes, the marked place is right" reasons status only: the values of a classification's reason, as terms provenance where the definitions come from or what they are adapted from

A vocabulary is the one text the docs, the taggers and the people who review their answers share: the model tagger (tagging.chat.v1) generates its questions from it and never paraphrases it, so the first fix for a wrong answer is to the definition. The catalog ships the vocabularies of role (every content role), status (with its reasons), production and the property schemes degraded, tiny, rotated, multi_column and form; verify checks that each defines a scheme of the data model and that role, status and the property schemes list exactly its values (data model). The content roles' PAGE-XML types, region labels and default layers stay in code (linecaster.data.policy.ROLES); the role vocabulary's page shows them.

items.title: Measurements live elsewhere
items.text:
linecaster is not a data repository: the catalog holds no measurements, and neither do the docs. An evaluation (a downstream project's, an evaluation project's) keeps its own records, in its own repository, and names what it measured by id and hash. linecaster provides the format and the tooling to produce them:

  • The evidence format (linecaster.evidence/3, linecaster.catalog.Evidence, schemas/evidence-3.json): one measurement per file, preset: id or recipe: id with its hash, context (for a preset measured inside a pipeline: the rest of it), source (own-run, card-claim, vendor-benchmark), dataset (repo@revision, or a description for claims), metrics, date, hardware, software (linecaster commit, server version, backend: in-process or served), run, notes. Claims are never measurements.
  • What a measurement names: the run record (OUT/run.yaml: the recipe and its hash, every component's parameters, pipeline_sha256, and catalog: every entry the run used, with its settings and hash) and the recipe and presets stamped on every annotator of every page.
  • What it measures: the page records (every transcription with its annotators' measurements: seconds, tokens, device), the traces (linecaster traces OUT: time per component and page) and the per-page and per-item files.

  • Ground truth and reference transcriptions: ManifestReader(existing_ocr=True) and the TranscriptionConverter read a library's own ALTO, PAGE-XML, hOCR or text into a named transcription (ocr_original, ground_truth, ...) of the page record, next to ocr_new; the writers turn page records into datasets (JSON Lines or Parquet page records, ALTO, PAGE-XML, hOCR, text).

  • Scoring (linecaster.evaluation, the evaluation): ground truths imported as transcriptions, rendered under the same rendering policy as the output they are compared with, compared through lanes (comparison strategies), scored per page into score records (linecaster.score/1) and aggregated into one evidence record, which names the run, the benchmark (linecaster.benchmark/2), the policy, the scorer (the linecaster release) and each lane by id and hash. A benchmark definition lives with the evaluation, like its evidence; linecaster ships the format, never a benchmark. linecaster score RUN TRUTH --benchmark FILE scores a run (score records and an evidence record, by default in RUN/scores/), linecaster evidence check FILES validates evidence records and linecaster evidence compare FILES puts those scored the same way side by side.

items.title: Release versioning: the index
items.text:
The catalog is versioned by the linecaster release, as a library's code is: entries carry no edition, there is no lock of released editions and no catalog migration. What an entry does is identified by the hash of its functional content (canonical_sha256):

  • a preset's: step, the model pin and every submodel pin (id, revision, files), engine, options, settings, labels, by_script (each strategy's id with its hash) and serve. Only what the YAML file states counts, so a new optional schema field changes no hash; the prose, provenance, support level and capabilities are not part of it;
  • a recipe's: its pipeline, each slot's preset with its hash and the options it states; the index also keeps pipeline_sha256, the hash of the pipeline its script builds from them (below);
  • a policy's: everything but its description;
  • conventions': the format, the resolved rules (each rule's id, match, decision, fields, who and place) and the normalizations the transcription embodies (transcription);
  • a normalization's: its rule; a strategy's: its normalizations, each with its hash, and its use;
  • a vocabulary's: everything but its description and provenance (a definition is what a model tagger is shown, so a changed definition is a change of behaviour).

linecaster catalog index writes every entry's hash to catalog.index (committed, never edited by hand); linecaster catalog verify fails when it is stale. So a change of an entry's behaviour is a visible line in a review's diff, and the release's CHANGELOG names every entry whose hash changed (Changed outputs). A run is reproducible by its release (linecaster==0.10.0 reruns 0.10.0's entries) and by its run record, which lists every entry it used with its settings and hash (catalog: kind, id, sha256, settings). Model pins (revision and file hashes) stay as they were: they identify weights, not behaviour of ours.

items.title: A recipe's expanded pipeline
items.text:
A recipe names a pipeline id, presets and options; what runs is the pipeline its script builds from them. catalog index builds each recipe's pipeline (its pipeline script with --recipe id on placeholder folders, in-process, one task) and records its pipeline_sha256, the hash a run record of that recipe names; verify builds it again, so a component, a parameter or a default that changed in code shows in the index.

Building it needs no engine: the describe mode (linecaster.execution.run.describe) builds the recipe's pipeline template (linecaster.templates) in the current process, and components and backends import no engine before warm_up(); a preset whose engine is not installed names the engine's class from the repository's engine packages (catalog.code). So verify runs in the core environment, and its hash is the one a run of the pipeline script with its engines records.

items.title: Conventions (conventions/<format>/<id>.yaml)
items.text:
What one public source's markup or export means (a wiki's templates and classes, a TEI customization, a repository's PAGE-XML profile), declaratively, in the format linecaster.conventions (linecaster.conventions). Its Markdown sidecar is required, with the headings ## Source, ## How the markup works, ## Not in the rules and ## Open questions: what the rules cannot say neatly.

Field Meaning id format the format whose importer applies it (html, xml, json, text, ...); its folder extends the parent entry, by id: the entry starts from the parent's resolved rules description, source what it is for and what it was written against (prose, not functional) rules each: id; match (kind: tree with a CSS selector and the conditions text, style, inside, not_inside; kind: json with a JSONPath, RFC 9535; kind: text with a regular expression); decision and its params (linecaster.conventions.decisions: remove with a reason, invisible, unwrap, component with a role, cell, picture, caption, note, edit, language, format, break, continues, runs_on, describe); by (people, who marked it in the source, or rule); before/after a rule id; why, decided, open disable a parent's rule id → why this source does not use it transcription the normalizations the source's transcription already embodies (normalization ids: long-s when it writes ſ as s); a child's list replaces its parent's. Importers copy it into Source.normalized; scoring warns where a lane does not apply one (evaluation)

Layering. A child's rule with a parent's id replaces it where it stands (or moves it, with before/after), a new id is added at the end (or before/after a rule), disable removes the parent's; every entry of a chain has the same format. Catalog.conventions(ref) resolves the chain into a ResolvedConventions: the rules in order, the chain (mediawiki>enwikisource), the normalizations of its transcription (the nearest entry's) and the hash of what the rules do (format, matches, decisions, fields, who, the transcription's normalizations; not the documentation). An importer records both in its annotator (conventions, conventions_sha256): two readings applied the same rules when the hashes are equal.

Checks (linecaster catalog verify): resolvable; every decision applied by its format's importer; the transcription's normalizations known; its prose and headings; across the children of one parent: a rule all of them repeat belongs in the parent (promotion), an override equal to what it replaces is redundant.

Conventions are the one kind of entry that names a source: they are declarative, opt-in (nothing applies them unless a run or ground truth names them), say what a source's markup means rather than what one dataset counts, hold no copied pages (tests use fixtures written for them), and keep the source's name inside the entry.

items.title: Steps, capabilities, labels
items.text:
Steps (STEPS): layout, lines, recognition, tables, formulas, whose engines run models, and the rule-based steps (RULE_STEPS) image (the working image), hierarchy (the hierarchy from type sizes), paragraphs (the paragraphs of the rows: structure, no text), document (the document) and import (a source document read into a transcription: the importers), and tagging (classifications in property schemes: taggers, rules and a panel of models). Recognition reads a unit (capabilities.unit): line (kraken, PaddleX, Tesseract), region (a VLM per layout region) or page (a VLM or a page engine reads the whole page: a page preset, which launch.py runs by name); a rule-based engine reads a page or an item (the pages of one item, in order). OCRD_STEPS maps the steps to OCR-D's functional steps for METS agents where OCR-D has one (image: preprocessing/optimization, hierarchy and tagging: layout/segmentation/classification, document: layout/analysis); the others are post-processing (recognition/post-correction).

What depends on the code belongs to the engine (capabilities on the class), e.g. kraken's word boxes with confidences. What depends on the weights belongs to the model or preset: languages, scripts, output format.

items.title: Engines
items.text:
An engine is a class registered under its id in the entry-point group linecaster.engines ("kraken.recognition.v1" = "linecaster_kraken:KrakenRecognitionEngine"), or one of linecaster's own (BUILTIN_ENGINES): chat.v1 (VLM presets, served only: SERVED_ONLY; the Chat backend), the single-region layout and the rule-based engines. It declares engine_id, step, Options (a Pydantic model whose fields have descriptions; the docs come from it) and capabilities, and takes the pin as weights (and submodel_weights), fetched and checked by linecaster.catalog.fetch. Engine packages carry code only; their presets and models are in this catalog.

chat.v1's Options (linecaster.engines.chat.ChatAdapter.Options) are what a run may set over a chat preset's settings (Chat(..., overrides=...), --set recognition.<option>=<value>): max_tokens, temperature and top_p over settings.sampling, repair_max_tokens and repair_temperature over settings.repair (the repair pass; off unless repair_max_tokens is above 0, which must then be larger than max_tokens; a list of rising caps is one repair pass each; lightonocr-3-0.8b sets [8192, 12288], the other presets leave it off), and repetition_detection over settings.sampling.repetition_detection (repetition detection: on by default wherever the preset's server is vLLM 0.17.0 or later, false off, true the defaults, repetition_detection.<field>=<value> for one of min_pattern_size, max_pattern_size, min_count; refused for another server).

Engine packages (engines/<engine>/: linecaster-kraken, linecaster-paddlex, linecaster-tesseract, linecaster-indra, linecaster-surya, linecaster-services) have versions of their own and a range of linecaster releases they work with (linecaster>=0.8,<0.10), and import from linecaster only the data model (linecaster.data) and the engine API (linecaster.engines.api): the Engine protocol, Capabilities, and the weight helpers weights_of (a model pin as weights), hf_file and hf_snapshot (a Hugging Face pin's files, checked) and model_entry (a model's catalog entry); tests/test_import_rule.py reads the packages with ast and fails on any other import. They are not on PyPI: a preset whose engine is not installed is a CatalogError that names the package that provides it and the pipeline scripts whose environments install it (catalog.code.install_hint). Each package has its tests in engines/<engine>/tests/ (conformance through linecaster.testing.check_engine, and its own units), run in an environment that has it (uv run tests/test_engines_catalog.py engines/<engine>/tests; the page engines' packages: uv run tests/test_page_engines_catalog.py engines/<engine>/tests, the environment of pipelines/transcribe_page.py).

items.title: Page engines and their services
items.text:
A page engine is an engine of the recognition step whose unit is the page (capabilities.unit: page): it gets the page image and returns the page's transcription, text-only, its raw output verbatim as a raw output (RawOutput), as a chat preset's completion is kept. PageRecognizer runs it like any model component (InProcess, or Served through linecaster serve); pipelines/transcribe_page.py is its pipeline. Where the engine talks to a service, its preset's serve block names it and VendorServer starts it in the task:

serve.server The service Fields vllm vllm serve <the model pin, fetched> --host --port <flags> --served-model-name <the Hugging Face id>, for an engine package that attaches to vLLM (surya.recognition.v1) version, image, flags vendor a vendor's page pipeline in its own image (falcon.recognition.v1, oxr.recognition.v1): the image's entrypoint image (by digest), command (the entrypoint), env, health (loopback URLs that must answer 200, in order), weights_dir (where the model pin is downloaded first, when the image reads the weights from a folder)

The engine's endpoint option (where its service is) is operational: presets leave it to its default (the service's loopback port), a pipeline sets it for a running service (--recognition-endpoint), and the pipeline's hash leaves it out.

items.title: The single-region layout
items.text: layout.single-region.v1 (linecaster.engines:SingleRegionLayoutEngine, preset single-region) is a layout engine without a model: one region covering the page image (label text, classified as a paragraph, id page; both options), alone in a reading order, by an annotator of kind rule and step layout. It has the model engines' call (__call__(image, transcription)), so LayoutDetector("single-region") runs it, and like the rule-based engines it is built in and runs in the pipeline's process only. pipelines/transcribe_modular.py --layout single-region reads a page as one region.

items.title: Rule-based engines
items.text:
The engines of the rule-based steps (strategies) live in linecaster.engines, are pure Python and run in the pipeline's process only (IN_PROCESS_ONLY; linecaster serve refuses them): image.webp-lossless.v1, hierarchy.ratios.v1, paragraphs.unicode.v1, document.linked.v1 and the by-script engine paragraphs.by-script.v1. None of them changes a text: they add structure (headings, paragraphs, links), and a strategy writes the text when it is written. Each has no weights; its Options turn the rules' thresholds into options whose defaults are the values the rules have always had, and it declares scripts: the ISO 15924 scripts it covers (Latn, Hebr, ...), "*" for all. The rules themselves stay in linecaster.text, linecaster.images and linecaster.formats; the engines are thin.

The call per unit (linecaster.engines.base): page unit __call__(t: Transcription, **options) -> Transcription; item unit __call__(pages: list[Transcription], **options) -> list[Transcription] (an item's pages in order; a page is an item of one page); the image step takes and returns the image's bytes (__call__(data, **options) -> (bytes, info)). Options given to a call override the engine's for that call. Each call appends an annotator (Annotator, kind rule) with its engine id, its options as settings and its counts as measurements; the component that runs it adds the preset and its hash, seconds and datetime. Composition is the exception: it renders the set as a document (linecaster.document) and adds no annotator and no annotation. Its item unit is item_document(pages, name, ...): an item's document is no transcription.

Their components take a preset (id) or an engine spec (InProcess("module:Class", **options)), with options over either, like model components but without a backend choice: ImageConverter(output_folder, preset) (image), HierarchyDetector(preset) (hierarchy), ParagraphBuilder(preset, unit="page"|"item") (paragraphs), DocumentComposer(preset, unit="page"|"item") (document). The presets of the squiddle recipe's rules: working-image, ratios, unicode-paragraphs, linked-document. Running text or the page as laid out is the presence of a ParagraphBuilder: the DocumentComposer composes from paragraphs when there are, else from lines (diplomatic composition).

items.title: Taggers
items.text:
The engines of the tagging step (taggers, linecaster.engines.tagging) classify zones in property schemes (rotated, tiny, multi_column, degraded, form) and other closed schemes, by the schemes' vocabularies. They are built in and run in the pipeline's process, called as the model steps' engines are (engine(image, transcription, page=None)), and the Tagger runs them (by preset, or by engine spec InProcess(...)). A tagger records a classification only where its evidence decides, on the narrowest target (a line, a region, the page), naming the raw output that holds the evidence.

  • tagging.geometry.v1 (GeometryTaggingEngine, preset geometry-tags): rules on geometry, annotator kind rule. rotated on lines (a vertical writing direction recorded, or a baseline, else a clearly elongated polygon, tilted by max_tilt degrees or more), tiny on lines (lower than tiny times the median height of the page's body text lines), multi_column on text regions (another text region beside it; no for a region alone that spans full_width of the page's text width). Its evidence (each line's tilt, height and ratio, the regions beside a region) is one raw output of format json; with decide_no: false it records only yes.
  • tagging.chat.v1 (ChatTaggingEngine): a panel of vision-language models behind OpenAI-compatible chat servers, annotator kind model. One question per target and scheme, generated from the vocabulary (the definition, what counts and what does not, the answers named after the property, cannot_tell, not_here; the reason asked for first, the answer last, as JSON), with the page and the target enlarged, its box drawn in red (views). Two members (panel, each a chat preset of the catalog or a served model) agree, or a third (referee) and the scheme's rule (settle: first_with_referee by default, majority, first) decide; an item no rule settles is recorded nowhere and written for review (review, JSON lines linecaster.tagging-review/1). Answers are cached under the hash of everything a member was shown and the model's revision ($LINECASTER_CACHE/tagging, else ~/.cache/linecaster/tagging). Every member's completion is a raw output; the annotator records the members' presets, revisions and sampling (never a server's address or key), the rules and each vocabulary's hash. The catalog ships no preset of it: which models make a panel, and in which order, is for a review of their answers to decide.

items.title: Scripts and dispatch
items.text:
A preset whose engine is a by-script engine names its strategies in by_script: an ISO 15924 code per script that needs its own rules, "*" for every other script.

id: hebrew-latin-recomposition
step: paragraphs
engine: paragraphs.by-script.v1
by_script:
  Hebr: hebrew-recomposition
  "*": unicode-paragraphs

engine_spec resolves them into the engine's strategies (each strategy's engine, options, id and hash). The engine (ScriptDispatch) routes each decision to the strategy of the script around it: for a decision at a row end (a division mark, the separator between two rows) the script of the last character before the row end that has one, else of the first after it (characters of the scripts Common and Inherited, such as spaces, hyphens, digits and combining marks, have none). A script without a strategy of its own goes to "*". Scripts are Unicode's Script property, matched with the regex package's \p{Script=...}. verify checks that every strategy is a preset of the same step and covers its script. (These by-script strategies are presets of a step; transcription strategies, the catalog kind, are another thing.)

items.title: Pipelines, recipes and launch.py
items.text:
Every pipeline script declares PIPELINE, its id: its file name with .v<n> (harvest.v1, transcribe_modular.v1, transcribe_vlm.v1, transcribe_page.v1, bind.v1, convert.v1, import_transcriptions.v1, score.v1). A script with slots also declares SLOTS (slot → option; the option is the step's name: --layout, --lines, --recognition, ...; the rule-based steps are slots too: transcribe_modular.v1 has --hierarchy, --paragraphs and --document, bind.v1 --paragraphs and --document; a slot left empty leaves its step out, e.g. no recomposition: the page stays as laid out). It has no default presets: the user fills every slot, or names a recipe (--recipe id), with single flags on top recorded as overrides in the run record (recipe: the id, the pipeline id, the hash and the overrides). The texts a run writes are no slot: --text <strategy>:<format> names each (a recipe may name them in its options).

The recipe: squiddle (transcribe_modular.v1: PP-DocLayoutV3, PP-OCRv6 line detection and kraken's PP-OCRv6 recognition, tables, formulas and the rule-based steps). The item stage (bind.v1) has no recipe: its presets are named (--paragraphs unicode-paragraphs --document linked-document, and the texts with --text). A recipe has its script, recipes/<id>.py (architecture): its environment, with exactly the engine packages its presets need, and its entry point. recipes/squiddle.py is the environment with kraken; pipelines/transcribe_modular.py leaves kraken out.

uv run launch.py NAME IMAGES OUT [options] launches a recipe or a page preset by name: a recipe runs its script recipes/<id>.py, a page preset the pipeline script of its kind (transcribe_vlm.v1 for chat page presets, transcribe_page.v1 for page engines' presets), each in its own environment, with --recipe or --recognition. serve and ray pass through for recipes. A preset that is one step of a pipeline gets a hint instead: the pipeline, the flag and the recipes that use it.

items.title: Support
items.text: core (maintained, validated), experimental (works, may change), legacy (kept resolvable; superseded_by: names the replacement).

items.title: Commands
items.text:
Command Does linecaster presets [--step STEP] lists the presets (and the recipes) linecaster catalog pin ID --hf REPO [--revision REV] pins a Hugging Face model: model entry, card, file hashes linecaster catalog pin ID --github OWNER/NAME --revision COMMIT --file F [--tag T] pins files of a GitHub repository linecaster catalog index writes catalog.index: every entry's hash, and each recipe's pipeline hash linecaster catalog verify checks the files (schema lines, prose next to its YAML file), the JSON Schemas against the models, cards, pins, the index (stale: a failure), conventions, recipes and their expanded pipelines linecaster catalog show REF the resolved functional content of a preset or recipe, with its hash linecaster catalog schemas [--out DIR] regenerates the JSON Schemas (default src/linecaster/catalog/schemas/) linecaster docs [--out docs] [--readme README.md] writes the generated docs (the catalog's pages among them; not in git, written before the site is built)

The catalog's generated pages are grouped by kind: docs/catalog/{engines, models, presets/<step>, pipelines, recipes, policies, conventions, normalizations, strategies}/ and an index. Engine and pipeline pages are read from the source (linecaster.catalog.code, with ast), so the engines need not be installed. The pages quote no measurements.

items.title: Compatibility
items.text: What linecaster keeps stable for downstream projects, pipelines and stored outputs, and how a change that breaks it is announced. Terms are the glossary's.

items.title: What counts as a breaking change
items.text:
A change is breaking when code, a command line, a stored file or a catalog reference that worked before stops working or starts to mean something else:

Surface Breaking Not breaking components a component renamed or removed; a constructor argument renamed, removed or made required; a default that changes what a run writes a new component; a new argument whose default keeps the old behavior backends InProcess, Served, Chat renamed or removed, or an argument as for components a new argument with a default that keeps the old behavior commands and flags a linecaster command or a pipeline script's option renamed, removed, or given another meaning or default a new command or option pipeline ids and slots a pipeline id or a slot renamed or removed, a slot's step changed a new pipeline script; a new slot that can stay empty data formats (page records, documents, run records, evidence, benchmarks, scores, samples) a field renamed, removed or given another meaning (a new format version, linecaster.page/5); a format version a reader no longer reads a new optional field (the version stays); a new version that its readers read together with the older ones, upgraded on load the run layout a folder or file name under OUT (pages/, rejects/, logs/, traces/, run.yaml) or its format changed a new file or folder the catalog a catalog id (model, preset, recipe, policy, conventions) renamed or removed; a field of an entry's file renamed or removed a new entry; a change of what an entry does (its hash in catalog.index changes), named in CHANGELOG.md under Changed outputs engines an engine id removed; an option renamed or removed, or a default changed (a new code id, .v2, instead) a new engine; a new option whose default keeps the old behavior (the same id) the Python API a public name renamed, removed or given another meaning in linecaster.data, linecaster.formats, linecaster.text, linecaster.images, linecaster.engines.api, linecaster.templates (the shapes), linecaster.execution.run (main, recipe, the helpers the shapes use) or linecaster.testing (its checks and markers) a new name the output files' contents a change of structure in the files a pipeline writes (ALTO, PAGE-XML, hOCR, Markdown, HTML, JSON) that breaks a reader of the old ones: other elements, attributes or fields better text; a new optional element or field resuming a run an unchanged command line gets another fingerprint (pipeline_sha256), so a run no longer continues in its folder without --new-pipeline a new operational parameter (left out of the fingerprint) how a run runs a run that succeeded before now fails or stops an operational default that leaves the outputs as they were (workers, tasks, threads, windows, timeouts, retries) dependencies and environment an extra or a dependency removed; a raised minimum (Python, uv, datatrove); another version of a pinned numerical library (torch, ONNX Runtime, a CUDA build), which can change the text a run produces a relock that moves only other packages; a new extra state shared by runs a broker layout or an HTTP policy field that older versions, running at the same time, no longer read alike a new optional field older versions ignore

Internal modules and names with a leading underscore, log messages, stats, the generated docs, tests/, CI, the docs build and NOTES.md are not part of it: a change there is never more than a patch.

items.title: While the version is 0.x
items.text: There is no deprecation period and there are no aliases: a breaking change takes effect in the release that makes it, and every breaking change is an upgrade note in CHANGELOG.md (what changed, who is affected, what to do), listed first.

items.title: Versions and releases
items.text:
Versions follow semantic versioning, with the 0.x convention that the minor number does what the major one does from 1.0 on. What a change bumps follows from the table above:

Change While 0.x From 1.0 fixes, performance, corrections of the docs, dependency updates that change no output patch patch new components, options, presets, recipes, commands or features that keep the old behavior patch minor breaking (any surface above; it needs an upgrade note) minor, collected (0.4.0 → 0.5.0) major

A release bumps by its largest change; patches are the rule. Ranges such as the engine packages' linecaster>=0.10,<0.11 then hold: every release inside them keeps what worked.

  • Breaking changes are collected, not released one by one. They are made on a branch and released together as one minor, proposed when the branch's work is finished. main carries only patch-level changes, so a fix can go out as a patch at any time.
  • A minor needs something users must change: its upgrade notes name it. A release with nothing to change is a patch.
  • When: when the maintainer decides; never one per piece of work or per commit. Finished work is merged into main and collects in CHANGELOG.md's Unreleased section until then. A release is proposed to the maintainer when it is due: the latest release is wrong or incomplete where its users meet it, a user or downstream project needs what only main has, or Unreleased holds a finished piece of work. A commit that changes only the README is no release.
  • How: the version in pyproject.toml and linecaster.__version__ (tests/test_version.py checks they agree), CHANGELOG.md's Unreleased section as ## <version> (<date>), the scripts relocked, an annotated tag v<version>, pushed (the docs workflow publishes <major>.<minor>). A minor bump while 0.x (a major one from 1.0) also widens the engine packages' linecaster range to the next one and bumps each engine package's patch version.
  • Engine packages version on their own by the same table, applied to their engines (ids, options, defaults).
  • A downstream project pins a linecaster release tag or follows main (a recipe script's raw URL), and versions, if at all, by its own interface, not by linecaster's numbers.
  • 1.0.0 is the maintainer's decision: from then on breaking changes get a deprecation period. No release reaches it on its own.

items.title: The catalog and the data formats
items.text:
The release versions the catalog (catalog): an entry is its id, and what it does is the hash of its functional content, listed in the committed catalog.index. A change of what an entry does shows in the index's diff and is named in CHANGELOG.md under Changed outputs, so a user knows what to run again; a run record names every entry it used with its settings and hash and the linecaster that ran it, which reproduces it. A reference from before 0.10 (id@N) resolves to the release's entry, with a warning. Engine and pipeline code ids keep their versions: an incompatible change of options or slots is a new id, and the old one stays registered.

Data formats keep their own versions, because their files outlive the code: a format's version rises only on an incompatible change, readers upgrade every older version on load and refuse an unknown one, writers write the current one, and every file names the linecaster that wrote it.

items.title: Conventions
items.text: Rules that hold across the repository. Each rule is followed by its reason. Terms are the glossary's.

items.title: Names
items.text:
What Pattern Examples component <Object><RoleNoun>; readers and writers <Object><Format>Reader / Writer LineRecognizer, HierarchyDetector, DocumentComposer, ItemAssembler, ManifestReader, PageJsonlWriter composite component <Purpose><RoleNoun> ModularTranscriber component base classes <Kind>Component PageComponent, ModelComponent, RuleComponent engine class <Provider><Step>Engine KrakenRecognitionEngine, UnicodeParagraphsEngine engine id <provider>.<step>.v<n> kraken.recognition.v1, paragraphs.unicode.v1 VLM adapter <Model>Adapter ChandraOCRAdapter pipeline script a verb, <verb>[_<kind>].py harvest.py, transcribe_modular.py, transcribe_vlm.py, transcribe_page.py, bind.py pipeline id the script's file name, .v<n> transcribe_modular.v1 slot and its flag the step's name --layout, --lines, --recognition step a noun for what the step produces or does layout, lines, recognition, paragraphs, document component package the step's name, or the plural of what the components are linecaster.components.layout, linecaster.components.readers component module the class's name in snake case line_recognizer.py transcription names ocr_new, ocr_original, ground_truth, or <source>

Reason: one pattern makes names guessable, and role nouns say what a component is in a pipeline. Pipeline scripts are verbs because they are what one runs.

items.title: Words
items.text: • Use the glossary's terms. A word has one meaning; a second meaning needs a qualifier ("content role", "HTTP block", "datatrove Document"). tests/test_vocabulary.py keeps retired terms out and checks that the glossary defines each term once. Reason: a reader who has learned a word once must be able to rely on it.

items.title: Prose
items.text:
These hold for the docs, docstrings and help texts.

  • Define a term where it first appears on a page, or link it to the glossary.
  • One idea per sentence. No parentheses inside parentheses.
  • Show an example before the rules that explain it.
  • Say what something is and does. Say what it is not only where a reader would otherwise mix two things up.
  • Concept pages (docs/concepts/) and tutorials (docs/start/) explain; reference pages (docs/reference/) are complete. Neither holds history or measurements: those are in CHANGELOG.md and NOTES.md.

Reason: the reference grew by adding qualifications to sentences, and became hard to read even for people who know the subject.

items.title: Spelling
items.text:
American English everywhere: code, flags, docs, commit messages (normalize, recognizer, behavior, license, color, catalog). Upstream text copied verbatim (model cards) keeps its spelling.

Reason: one spelling for everything typed, matching Python and its ecosystem.

items.title: YAML and Markdown
items.text:
• Data that tools read is YAML; prose for people is Markdown. A catalog entry is <id>.yaml, optionally with <id>.md next to it; tools never read the Markdown. Reason: Markdown renders cleanly, data validates, and diffs of the two do not mix.
  • Every YAML file names its format twice: a first line # yaml-language-server: $schema=<relative path to src/linecaster/catalog/schemas/<kind>-<n>.json> (editors validate and complete) and a field schema: linecaster.<kind>/<n> (tools check it). Reason: mistakes show while editing, not at run time.
  • The schemas are generated from the pydantic models (model_json_schema()) into src/linecaster/catalog/schemas/ (shipped with the package; linecaster catalog schemas rewrites them), and a test fails when a committed schema differs from a fresh one. The pydantic models are the only source of truth. Reason: one definition, used by tools and editors alike.
  • YAML is YAML 1.2, read with ruamel.yaml: true/false are the only booleans (NO stays a string), duplicate keys are errors, and tools that write files back keep their comments.
  • An entry's hash covers its functional content (what changes behavior: step, engine, options, pins, settings, labels, serving), read from the YAML; catalog.index lists every hash, so a change of behavior shows in review and goes into the CHANGELOG's Changed outputs. The Markdown prose and descriptive fields (support, provenance) are not part of it; git keeps their history.

Schemas: the catalog's kinds without a version (preset, recipe, model, policy, conventions, normalization, strategy: the release versions them), the data formats with theirs (benchmark-2, evidence-3, and the older evidence formats readers upgrade, run-record-2, page-6, document-2). Stored page records name their format in a schema field of their row (linecaster.page/6).

items.title: Docstrings
items.text:
Google style, checked by tests/test_docstrings.py (with ast, no extra tool) for every public component, built-in engine, backend, serializer, build, run_pages, runtime.run.main, public function of linecaster.catalog and public name of linecaster.engines.api and linecaster.testing:

  • Summary line: what the component or function does, in the present tense, starting with a verb, one sentence: "Recognizes the text of every line with its engine." It may wrap; it ends at the first blank line. The component index and the README's component table show it.
  • Body: the contract in words (what it reads, adds and replaces), edge cases, what it records (annotators, stats, errors on the page).
  • Args: names every parameter of the signature (a class documents its constructor's), and no other: one entry each, name: meaning, the effect of the default, constraints., continuation lines indented. Several parameters may share an entry (data_folder, paths_file, ...: datatrove's BaseDiskReader arguments.), as datatrove's inherited reader and writer arguments do; **kwargs is an entry too. A class that keeps its base's constructor keeps its base's Args:.
  • Example: (indented Python code) is required for runtime.run.main, build(), the serializers (to_alto, from_alto, ...) and the public functions of linecaster.catalog; optional for components, whose generated pages show it.
  • Inline code in double or single backticks; the generated pages render both as code. Engine options are described in their Options model (Field(description=...)), not in a docstring.

Reason: the generated component pages come from the docstrings, so the reference is only as good as they are, and a test keeps them complete as signatures change.

items.title: Contracts
items.text:
• Every component declares its unit and what it reads, adds and replaces (pipelines). A part of the record is added by one component only, unless a later component declares that it replaces it. Reason: the builder can then check a pipeline before it runs and derive its graph.
  • Components are pure transforms of their unit; only readers and writers know about tasks, ranks and files. Reason: the same components run on any executor and in run_pages().

items.title: Tests
items.text:
• Every built-in engine passes linecaster.testing.check_engine and every public component check_component (tests/testing/test_conformance.py); an engine package checks its engines the same way in engines/<engine>/tests/. Reason: the protocol and the contracts hold for every implementation, not only the ones a pipeline happens to run.
  • A test that needs a CUDA device is marked gpu, one that downloads weights or reaches the internet network, one over about 10 s slow (--strict-markers). Reason: the default run skips what a machine cannot run, and CI runs what a CPU can.
  • Tests use the fake engines, the fake chat server and the fake service of linecaster.testing, not copies of their own. Reason: one fake per step behaves the same in every test.

items.title: Tracing
items.text:
• Tracing (OpenTelemetry) is always on. Spans per task always; spans per page for a trace sample chosen by page id, plus every page that failed. Reason: where a run loses time is only visible per page and across processes.
  • A page carries its trace context from the reader on; components open spans as children of the page's context, never of "the current span". Reason: pages are interleaved in the stream.
  • Attributes are identifiers and numbers under linecaster.*, never content (text, images). Reason: content belongs in the rows, which the page id links to.
  • Traces are written to OUT/traces/ and, when the standard OTEL_* variables are set, exported to a backend (tracing).

items.title: Telemetry
items.text: linecaster sends nothing to anyone that the user did not configure. No usage data, no phoning home, not even opt-in. Reason: libraries and archives run it on their own infrastructure under their own rules.

items.title: Logging
items.text: loguru (datatrove's), with {placeholder} templates and named values, never formatted strings: logger.warning("page {page_id} failed in {component}: {error}", page_id=..., component=..., error=...) (the values land in the record's extra). JSON lines on Jobs: the pipeline scripts set LINECASTER_LOG_JSON=1 in their Jobs, where the tasks (linecaster.execution.jobs.JobsExecutor) and linecaster serve log with loguru's serialize=True (linecaster.execution.logs). Log records carry trace_id and span_id. Reason: logs can be filtered and joined to traces.

items.title: Errors
items.text: Library code raises the classes of linecaster.errors (PipelineConfigError, CatalogError, PageError, ServerError, all LinecasterError), never SystemExit; only the command line (linecaster, a pipeline script's main) turns them into exit codes, and a test fails on any other exit. Pure functions of the data model, the formats and the text transforms keep Python's own ValueError for a wrong argument. Reason: a downstream project that embeds linecaster can catch what went wrong, and a run's exit code says whether anything was launched.

items.title: Secrets
items.text: A credential is never a value in a pipeline: it is an EnvVar("NAME") (linecaster.secrets), read in the task. Reason: datatrove pickles the pipeline for every executor, and the run record lists every component's parameters.

items.title: Changes
items.text: CHANGELOG.md in the Keep a Changelog format, with upgrade notes first. NOTES.md is the log of measurements and decisions; reference documents (docs/reference/) describe what is, without history.

items.title: The data model
items.text: linecaster.data holds what is read from a page and how it is rendered; linecaster.data.page the page record it travels in. A stored page record names its format in its row's schema: linecaster.page/6. Importing linecaster.data needs neither datatrove nor saturate nor an engine.

items.title: Principles
items.text:
1. Raw output is kept. What a model answered (a completion, an engine's native result) is stored verbatim, once per request, next to what linecaster parsed from it (RawOutput).
  2. Nothing is discarded or overwritten. Every step adds annotations; a correction, a removal, a relabelling is a new annotation that refers to the one it is about. A page record holds everything any step said, and who said it.
  3. The record holds the text as read. A reading is what the model or the source gave, exactly, not even in NFC. No step changes it or stores a derived form of it: a normalization (NFC, the long s, ligatures, a division mark removed, rows joined) is applied when a text is written, by the transcription strategy the text names (linecaster.document.strategy), and never by default. Edits are the source's own (an editor's correction, a word the source marks as divided).
  4. Rendering is a recorded, overridable policy. Which annotations end up in which text (body, page furniture, notes, metadata, nowhere) is decided by a rendering policy at rendering time, never by a parser or a step. The policy is a catalog entry; run records and evidence name it with its hash.
  5. Definitions generic, vocabularies specific. The classes hold any input (a scanned book, a manuscript, a born-digital PDF, a newspaper issue); what a region is, how it was made and what a range is are words from vocabularies borrowed from the standards (PAGE-XML first), extended where they lack a word.
  6. Records are lean. Shared things are stored once per page and referred to by number (annotators, raw outputs); geometry is numbers; parts are nested where they never move (words in readings, glyphs in words); renderings (documents, texts) are written out, not stored; defaults are not written.

The concepts are borrowed from IIIF Presentation 3 and the W3C Web Annotation model (annotations with a target, a motivation and a body), PAGE-XML (region types, production) and PROV (derivation), under linecaster's names; the mappings are below (mappings). Exports conform to each standard.

items.title: Units
items.text:
Class Is Key Item a named, ordered container of one or more pages item_id Page one page of an item: its image and its annotation sets page_id PageImage the image a page's coordinates refer to: its location, size, format and hashes DocumentRange a unit of continuous content within or across items (a work, an article, a letter); see ranges id
