Detection often splits one printed line into several lines of one row. classification A value of one scheme given to a target (Classification): content role, production, heading level, language, script. content role What a region or line is: paragraph, heading, marginalia, footnote, header, page number. Always written with "content". region label The coarser word layout models use for a region (text, title, table, picture). Each content role maps to one. edit Another form of a target's text that the source itself states (Edit): corrected, expanded, regularized, or the whole of a divided word. The original text stays. paragraph Running text built from the rows of lines (Paragraph), with the decisions that made it. document The reader-facing result for a page or an item (linecaster.document.Document): titles, headings, paragraphs, tables and notes in order. Built from transcriptions, written as HTML, Markdown, text or JSON. datatrove's class of the same name is always written "datatrove Document". block One unit of a document (Block): a heading, a paragraph, a list item, a caption, a table, a picture. rendering Anything written from an annotation set: a document, ALTO, PAGE-XML, hOCR, a IIIF annotation page, a text. Renderings are written out and never stored in the page record. rendering policy A catalog entry that decides which annotations go into which layer of a rendering. It changes no text. layer Where a rendering puts content: body, furniture (running heads, page numbers), notes, background, invisible, metadata or none. normalization One named change of a text, as a catalog entry: nfc, long-s, flow. Nothing is normalized unless a strategy says so. strategy A named, ordered list of normalizations, as a catalog entry (latin-historic). It is applied when a text is written (--text latin-historic:md), never to what is stored. Several joined by + make an unnamed one (nfc+long-s+flow). literal The strategy that changes nothing: the readings exactly as given. text A written text of a page or an item: a strategy and a format (literal:txt). flow The normalization that joins the rows of a block into running text. A division mark that nothing resolved is kept. division mark A hyphen the typesetter added where a word was divided at a line end. script A writing system, by its ISO 15924 code (Latn, Hebr). A uv script is always a "pipeline script" or "recipe script".

items.title: Evaluation
items.text: Term Meaning ground truth A transcription made or checked by people, which runs are scored against. benchmark A definition of how runs are scored against one ground truth: the dataset, the pages, the rendering policy, the lanes and the metrics. evaluation Runs scored under a benchmark, with their score records and evidence records. An evaluation lives in its own repository. score record One page's counts for one text and one lane. Every rate is derived from the counts. evidence record A measurement of a preset or recipe with its source: the run, the benchmark and the scoring it was measured with. Kept by an evaluation, never in the catalog. element A part of a page that is scored on its own: a region's text, a table or a formula. match group Elements of the ground truth and of the output that were matched to each other and are compared as wholes. lane A strategy both sides of a comparison go through before they are counted (diplomatic, reading, alnum). stratum The pages or elements that share one value of a dimension (content role, language, script, a tag). Rates are reported per stratum. slice The pages of a benchmark whose ground truth has tables, formulas, or neither, with rates of their own. split A named share of a ground truth's items (test, train). Every page of an item is in the same split. export A ground truth and a run written as another project's benchmark files (linecaster export omnidocbench).

items.title: Running at scale
items.text:
Explained in pipelines.

Term Meaning item shard A folder of page records that holds every page of a set of items, so that a later stage reads whole items. observer A callback before and after each unit of a component: progress, taps, tracing. tap An observer that writes the page records as they leave a given component (--tap-after). partial run A run of part of a pipeline: up to a component (--until) or from the page records after one (--after). item rank, page rank An item's place in the sample order, and a page's place within its item. Both come from a hash of the seed and the ids. stratified sample A sample whose pages are chosen separately for each stratum. secret reference EnvVar("NAME"): a credential named by its environment variable. It is read in the task and never stored. image warning A fault in an image file that is read around and recorded, without failing the page: for example an optional PNG chunk with a wrong checksum, or EXIF that cannot be read. working image The image preset working-image: lossless WebP at full resolution, 8-bit sRGB. manifest An item's list of its pages and their files: a IIIF Presentation manifest or a METS document. resource A remote file of an item or a page (a catalogue record, a manifest, OCR, an image), fetched and kept as a raw copy with a fetch record.

items.title: Vision-language models
items.text:
Explained in the catalog.

Term Meaning pass One request for a page. A page has more than one pass only when it is repaired. repair pass A further request for a page whose completion stopped at its token limit, with a higher limit. The page keeps the first completion that finished. repetition detection vLLM's guard against a completion that loops: the server ends it early. Such a page is not repaired. grounding A model's mode that labels and locates every text block of the page while it transcribes it. linecaster makes one region per block. adapter The code that talks to one VLM family over the OpenAI-compatible API: its request and its parsing (linecaster.engines.chat). page engine An engine whose unit is the page: it reads the whole page and returns its transcription (PageRecognizer runs it). service The server a page engine talks to that is neither linecaster serve nor a chat server: a vendor's own image. VendorServer starts it.

items.title: Ground-truth sources
items.text:
Explained in the catalog and in evaluation.

Term Meaning importer An engine of the import step: it reads a source file into a transcription. source file The file, record or wiki page an importer reads (SourceFile). conventions A catalog entry that says what one public source's markup means, as rules an importer applies. match Where a conventions rule points: a CSS selector, a JSONPath or a regular expression. decision What a conventions rule says the matched thing is: remove, text_block, note, edit, cell. Also: one choice the ParagraphBuilder made at a row end, always written "paragraph decision". coverage What an importer's conventions handled on a page: the matches per rule and what no rule matched. anchor Where a zone's text comes from in the source text: a character range. line image An image of one line with its text, as line-level ground-truth datasets give them. tokenizer How the word metrics cut a text into words (uax29, whitespace, characters). A model's tokenizer is always written "the model's tokenizer".

items.title: Classification schemes
items.text:
Explained in the data model.

Term Meaning vocabulary A catalog entry that defines the values of one classification scheme. property scheme A classification scheme whose values are yes and no: degraded, tiny, rotated, multi_column, form. tag A classification in a property scheme, with its basis. No tag does not mean no. tagger An engine of the tagging step: rules on geometry, or a panel of models. production How content was made: printed, typewritten, handwritten, stamped, born digital. writing direction The direction a page or block is written in: horizontal-lr, horizontal-rl, vertical-rl, vertical-lr. motivation Why an annotation was made (segmenting, transcribing, classifying, ...). The W3C Web Annotation term. shape Geometry without an annotator of its own (Shape): a word, a glyph, a cell. word, glyph A word of a reading, and one character of a word, each with its box and confidence. link A cross-reference between two annotations (Link): caption of, note of, continues. range A logical unit of content across pages (Range): a chapter, a section, an article. reference A string naming an annotation in the same set (Ref). measurements Numbers an annotator records for a page: seconds, tokens, device. XY-cut, XY-Cut++ The two ways linecaster computes a reading order when the layout model gives none. cross-layout region A text region that spans several columns: longer than 1.3 times the median region and overlapping two or more others horizontally. XY-Cut++ sets it aside before cutting.

items.title: Fetching
items.text:
Explained in HTTP and broker.

Term Meaning HTTP policy How a run's requests go out, from one YAML file (--http-policy): rate limits, retries, the User-Agent, the proxies, and a host entry for each host that differs. host entry The settings of one host in an HTTP policy. They replace the general ones. HTTP block A host turning a request away because of where it comes from: a 429 by default (block_on). The proxy is left out for that host, or the worker's requests to it pause. An HTTP block does not count as a failed attempt. Always written with "HTTP" or of a proxy or host; a bare "block" is a document's. unexpected HTML A successful response with an HTML page where an image, XML or JSON was expected. A failed attempt by default. pause A time in which a worker sends no request to a host and its requests wait. breaker A guard against an outage: when most recent attempts got a server error, requests pause until the host answers again. broken proxy A proxy that failed several attempts in a row itself. It is left out for every host for a while. proxies per worker How many proxies of a list one worker holds at a time. broker A shared folder through which workers on any machine agree on who uses which shared thing, such as a proxy. It has no server. lease A worker's claim on one thing in the broker. It expires unless renewed. mark A note in the broker that something is unavailable until a time. worker identity Who holds leases in the broker: a numbered place on a machine, which outlives the processes that fill it.

items.title: Tracing
items.text:
Explained in tracing.

Term Meaning trace, span OpenTelemetry's terms. A trace is one page's or one task's path through a run, made of spans. traced pages The pages that get a trace: a fixed share chosen by page id (--trace-share), plus every page that failed. trace context A page's traceparent, given by the reader. The page's spans are its children. task span A span of the task's own work: a warm-up, a server start, a writer's flush. gap The time a component had no page in it between its first page and its last.

items.title: Contributing
items.text:
Explained in conventions and compatibility.

Term Meaning engine API What an engine package may import from linecaster besides the data model: linecaster.engines.api. fake engine A deterministic CPU engine for tests, one per step (linecaster.testing). conformance check check_engine and check_component: the tests every engine and every component must pass. generated docs The pages linecaster docs writes from code, docstrings and the catalog. Never edited by hand and not in git. breaking change A change after which code, a command line, a stored file or a catalog reference stops working or means something else. upgrade note The CHANGELOG entry for a breaking change: what changed, who is affected, what to do.

items.title: The name
items.text: A linecaster is a hot-metal typesetting machine that casts whole lines of type. linecaster makes a new, digital edition of a printed item, line by line.

items.title: HTTP
items.text:
How linecaster's readers fetch over http(s) (linecaster.net.http, linecaster.net.proxies, linecaster.net.policy): the defaults, what a block is and how each path answers it, unexpected HTML, retries, and the HTTP policy file that changes all of it per host. Terms are the glossary's; how workers share the proxies is in the broker, how runs choose their workers in pipelines.

The principle: the defaults follow the HTTP standards (a 429 with its Retry-After, the retryable statuses, Retry-After as seconds or an HTTP-date); anything learned from one site or CDN (a block page served with 200, a 403 that means "this IP", a block that lasts three days) is opted into per host in an HTTP policy.

items.title: The defaults
items.text: Setting Default What it does user_agent HF-Research/1.0 (datatrove's, USER_AGENT) the User-Agent of every request; random_user_agent (--random-user-agent) a random browser one per task instead timeout 300 s each phase of a request (connect, read, write, pool) max_keepalive_connections 16 idle connections kept open for reuse max_retries 4 retries after the first attempt (5 attempts; 0: one) retry_wait_min, retry_wait_max 2 s, 60 s the wait after the n-th failed attempt: retry_wait_min * 2**(n-1), at most retry_wait_max (2, 4, 8, 16 s) retry_after_max 300 s the longest Retry-After a retry honors on the direct path attempt_timeout, attempt_min_rate 15 s, 50,000 bytes/s the deadline per attempt: 15 s plus 1 s per 50 kB the response declares retryable statuses 408, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 520-524 (RETRYABLE_STATUS_CODES) tried again; every other 4xx and 5xx fails at once rate_limits none N/S windows, at most N requests in any S seconds, all at once: per worker direct, per proxy through proxies block_on [429] (BLOCK_ON) what is a block (statuses and html) stop_on [] what stops the run at once (statuses and html) max_pause 6 h (MAX_PAUSE) the most a worker's requests to a host wait in all since the host's last successful response: in pauses direct, for a usable proxy through proxies (below) first wait of a block 60 s (BLOCK_FIRST_WAIT) a block without Retry-After: 60 s, then twice the last wait on each repeat shortest block 1 s (PAUSE_MIN_WAIT) whatever Retry-After says (0, a date gone by) proxies: block_ttl 3600 s (BLOCK_TTL) the longest a blocked proxy is left out without Retry-After: the ceiling of the doubling, and of a broken proxy's proxies: broken_after 3 (BROKEN_AFTER) proxy errors in a row before a proxy is broken proxies: broken_ttl 300 s (BROKEN_TTL) a broken proxy's first time out, doubling, at most block_ttl proxies: per_worker share how many proxies of the list a worker holds (broker)

items.title: Blocks
items.text:
A block means "this IP was turned away", through a proxy or direct: the server only sees an IP. What counts as a block is declared once for both paths (block_on: statuses, and html for an HTML page where another format was expected). The connection decides the reaction:

direct (one IP) through proxies a response in block_on the worker's requests to that host wait (a pause) for Retry-After, or else 60 s, doubling on each repeat; requests to other hosts go on; the run stops when the wait would be too long (past max_pause since the host's last successful response) the proxy is marked for that host (Retry-After, or else 60 s doubling up to block_ttl) and the request goes on at once through another proxy, without using up an attempt a response in stop_on the run stops at once the run stops at once no usable proxy (none) the requests to that host wait for a block to end or a proxy to free up; the run stops when the waits would pass max_pause since the host's last successful response connection errors the host's errors: retries and the breaker the proxy's errors: they count toward broken_after, then the proxy is left out for every host

How long a block lasts is one function for both paths (linecaster.net.http.block_wait): with Retry-After (seconds or an HTTP-date) exactly that, at least 1 s; without it 60 s, then twice the last wait for each block that repeats (for that host, and through proxies for that proxy at that host), at most block_ttl through proxies and max_pause direct. Direct, the worker keeps each host's doubling in memory (it owns its IP); through proxies the doubling travels with the proxy in the broker's marks, so a worker that claims a released proxy continues it (broker). The doubling starts again at 60 s after a successful response from the host (through proxies: through that proxy), or after a quiet period: when the next block comes more than the last wait after the last block there ended (linecaster.net.http.doubling). A response to a request sent before a block that still holds changes nothing. A block is never an attempt: the request that got it is tried again after the pause (direct) or at once through another proxy, with all its retries left.

A broken proxy fails attempts itself (a proxy error, no connection to the proxy, PROXY_ERRORS) broken_after times in a row: it is left out for every host, first for broken_ttl, twice as long each time it breaks again before it carries an answer, at most block_ttl. A timeout reading the server's answer is a slow server, not a broken proxy: it is retried and leaves the proxy in. Blocks and broken proxies are marks in the broker, so every worker that shares it leaves the proxy out, and continues their doubling when it claims the proxy.

items.title: max_pause
items.text: max_pause is one count on both paths, per worker and host (linecaster.net.http.PauseTotal): the time the worker's requests to the host have spent waiting since the host's last successful response, direct in pauses (the length each block adds), through proxies waiting for a usable proxy (the time no proxy was usable there). Once the next wait would take it past max_pause (a block whose wait is known, the first proxy block that ends), or it has passed it (waiting for proxies other workers hold), the run stops with StopRequests, whose message says how long the host's requests waited. A successful response from the host starts it again, through any proxy. Each host counts for itself: a pause at one host neither holds nor counts against the requests to another. The breaker's waits (a server that fails) do not count: each request waits one out a few times, then fails.

items.title: Unexpected HTML
items.text:
A successful response (2xx) with an HTML page where an image, XML, JSON or a manifest was expected is unexpected HTML: an error page served with 200, a soft 404, a login page after a redirect, a CDN's challenge. The readers say what they expect (HTTPFetcher.submit's expect: images, manifests, ALTO files, resources whose kind or URL names a format). A body is HTML (linecaster.net.http.is_html, read after a UTF-8 byte order mark, whitespace and <!-- --> comments) when it starts as an HTML document (<!doctype html, <html), whatever its Content-Type says; or when it is labelled text/html and is empty, plain text (an error message), XHTML, or starts with an HTML element (<head>, <body>, <div>, ...: HTML_ELEMENTS). A body labelled text/html that starts as data is data a server mislabelled and passes: JSON, an XML declaration or another root element (ALTO, METS, MODS without a declaration), an image (DATA_MAGIC). ResourceReader checks its resources with the same rule. An error status with an HTML body is that status: a 503 maintenance page is a 503, retried as one.

By default unexpected HTML is a failed attempt, on both paths: it counts, is retried after the backoff, and is traced 200-html. After the last attempt the fetch fails with UnexpectedHTML, whose message names the expected format and the content type (an HTML page (text/html; charset=utf-8, 1234 bytes) where an image was expected: URL); through proxies as the cause of MaxRetriesExceeded (after 5 attempts: an HTML page ...). With html in block_on it is a block instead (above), with html in stop_on it stops the run.

items.title: Retries and deadlines
items.text:
A request is tried up to max_retries + 1 times (HTTPFetcher._attempts, one loop for both paths). A transport error (a timeout, a broken connection, a proxy error, an attempt past its deadline), a retryable status and unexpected HTML are tried again after retry_wait_min * 2**(n-1) seconds (at most retry_wait_max); on the direct path at least as long as the response's Retry-After asks (at most retry_after_max); through proxies the next attempt goes out through another proxy, without it. Any other status fails at once (httpx.HTTPStatusError); a 404 first tries the page's fallback URL, if it has one, with attempts of its own. Retries used up raise the last error (direct) or MaxRetriesExceeded naming it (through proxies). Each attempt must be done within its deadline: attempt_timeout plus 1 s per attempt_min_rate bytes the response declares, counted from when it goes out, after the rate limits; one that takes longer is cut and retried.

Each fetcher also has a breaker (linecaster.net.http.Breaker): when most recent attempts got a server error, its requests pause, a probe goes out now and then, and the first answer that is not a server error ends the pause. Unexpected HTML is not an answer for it (it would keep the breaker closed while a host serves only error pages); a resource that fails as unexpected HTML counts once as a server error.

items.title: Trace entries
items.text: Every fetch records its attempts (the fetch record's tries, the http.tries of a page's linecaster.http.fetch span, tracing): 200 (or another status) for a response read whole, 200-cut for one cut by the deadline per attempt, 200-html for unexpected HTML, no-response for none (a timeout, a connection or proxy error). A block is traced with its status (429) but does not count among the attempts a failed fetch names. The record also has the time spent waiting for the rate limits (wait_seconds) and in pauses (pause_seconds).

items.title: The HTTP policy
items.text:
--http-policy FILE (linecaster.net.policy.HTTPPolicy) gives a run's requests their settings from one YAML file, in three levels, each inheriting from the one above. It holds for every reader that fetches over http(s), the same way (linecaster.net.policy.Fetchers): --items, --parquet with http(s) image URLs, --manifests (the manifests, their images and OCR files) and --pages (the images it fetches again).

# 1. general: every request, direct or through a proxy
rate_limits: ["100/60", "2/1"]     # per worker direct, per proxy through proxies
attempt_timeout: 120
max_retries: 6
random_user_agent: true            # or user_agent: TEXT
block_on: [429]                    # default [429]; 4xx/5xx statuses and `html`
stop_on: []                        # statuses and `html`; never also in block_on
max_pause: 6h
# 2. proxies: only for requests through the proxy list; inherits level 1
proxies:
  file: proxies.txt
  per_worker: share                # share | 1 | N
  block_ttl: 3600                  # a blocked proxy without Retry-After: the ceiling of the doubling
  broken_after: 3                  # proxy errors in a row before it is left out
  broken_ttl: 300                  # a broken proxy's first time out, doubling, at most block_ttl
# 3. hosts: per host, the same two levels; each field overrides the one above
hosts:
  catalog.example.org:
    direct: true
    rate_limits: ["25/60"]
    stop_on: [html]
  images.example.org:
    proxies: {block_ttl: 72h}
broker: s3://bucket/broker         # root only

Durations are seconds or a number with s, m, h or d (72h). A host's settings are, from the lowest precedence up:

  1. linecaster's defaults (above);
  2. the file's level 1, at its root;
  3. the run's own options: --rate-limit, --proxies (the proxy list's file), --user-agent, --random-user-agent;
  4. the host's level 1, under hosts:.

The proxies: section applies only on the proxy path: the root's, then the host's, field by field (a host's proxies: {block_ttl: 72h} keeps the root's file). A field at a host replaces the root's, it does not merge into it (stop_on: [403] at a host drops the root's stop_on). direct: true at a host means no proxies there, neither a list nor the environment's (HTTPS_PROXY); direct: false undoes a direct root. broker is the folder through which the workers share the proxies and their blocks, at the root only (default OUT/logs/broker). The checks at startup: something in both block_on (or its default) and stop_on is refused (to stop on a 429, write block_on: [] with stop_on: [429]); hosts that use one proxy list must agree on its per_worker; an unknown field is an error. Each host's settings get their own fetcher, so each host its own rate limits, breaker, pause and window.

A run states the rules that hold per host and path before it starts (HTTPPolicy.describe, in the run's notes), defaults and opt-ins alike, e.g. catalog.example.org: direct, 25/60 per worker, 4 retries, blocks on 429: the worker waits Retry-After, else 1 min doubling, and stops when the wait would pass 6 h, stops on html.

items.title: Fields of earlier versions
items.text:
Fields of earlier versions are refused at startup with a PipelineConfigError that names the line to write instead:

Field Write instead pause_on: [429, 503] block_on: [429, 503] blacklist_on: [403] block_on: [429, 403] (with the statuses of pause_on, if any) blacklist_ttl: 72h proxies: {block_ttl: 72h} blacklist_threshold: 2 proxies: {broken_after: 2} proxies: proxies.txt proxies: {file: proxies.txt} proxies_per_worker: 1 proxies: {per_worker: 1}

items.title: A CDN-protected host
items.text:
A host behind a CDN that answers a turned-away IP with a challenge page (HTML with 200) and keeps an IP blocked for an hour, where one proxy error already means the proxy is unusable, gets the strict reaction back per host:

proxies: {file: proxies.txt}
hosts:
  images.example.org:
    block_on: [429, html]          # a challenge page is a block: the proxy is left out, the request goes on
    proxies:
      block_ttl: 3600              # left out up to an hour without Retry-After
      broken_after: 1              # one proxy error in a row: broken

Direct, the same block_on: [429, html] makes the worker wait on a challenge page as on a 429, or stop when the wait would be too long.

items.title: Pipelines: contracts and the builder
items.text: A pipeline is a list of components (datatrove PipelineSteps) and composites. Before it runs, the builder (linecaster.execution.builder) checks the components' contracts, expands the composites, and cuts the pipeline into stages. Every pipeline script goes through it (linecaster.execution.run). Terms are the glossary's.

items.title: Contracts
items.text:
Every component returns its contract from contract() (linecaster.core.contract):

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Part:
    name: str                  # a name of PARTS, or "*" (every part)
    transcription: str | None  # ocr_new, ocr_original, ...; None: page-level (image, metadata, transcription_file)
                               # or the item record's

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Contract:
    unit: str                  # "page", "item" (what the input stream carries) or "any" (servers)
    unit_out: str | None       # set when the component changes the stream's unit (binder: page -> item, splitter: back)
    reads: frozenset[Part]
    adds: frozenset[Part]
    replaces: frozenset[Part]
    removes: frozenset[Part]   # parts the component does not pass on (gone for every later component)
    role: str                  # reader, writer, server, model, transform, binder, splitter, validator, composite
  • The vocabulary is PARTS in linecaster.catalog.schema: image, metadata and transcription_file (a library's own transcription delivered with the page, as a document media) (page-level), what presets produce (PRODUCES: regions, reading_order, lines, baselines, text, words, word_confidences, line_confidences, tables, formulas, markdown, html, doctags, layout_json, latex), and line_regions, hierarchy, paragraphs, document. A part is written transcription:name (ocr_new:lines); ocr_original:* is every part of a transcription.
  • Simple components declare class attributes (unit, role, parts_read, parts_added, parts_replaced, parts_removed) that the default contract() of Contracted reads; page-level names stay page-level, the others belong to the component's transcription. Components whose parts depend on their options compute contract().
  • Model components read the page image (recognition also lines, tables and formulas regions) and add their preset's capabilities.produces: the preset of the InProcess backend (preset), of the Served backend (preset, set by runtime.run.engines) or of the Chat backend; without a preset the engine class's capabilities (read from its source in the repository, else from the class); without either the step's default. The chat recognizers add text too, RegionRecognizer also lines (and replaces lines and text: the transcription's earlier lines are replaced).
  • Readers add image and metadata; ManifestReader(existing_ocr=True) also transcription_file, which the TranscriptionConverter reads (adding ocr_original:*); PageRecordReader what provides= declares (["ocr_new:lines", ...]), or anything (*, reads after it are not checked) when it declares nothing. With fetch_images=False it brings no image.
  • Writers read what they write and add nothing (ImageFilesWriter replaces metadata: the image's URI then names its copy; PageFileWriter: lines for hOCR, ALTO and PAGE, text for md and txt, document for HTML and JSON, image for plots). Servers have role server and unit any.
  • The ItemAssembler changes the unit from pages to items, the ItemSplitter back: an item record holds its page records, so what the pages carried stays available across either (the checks carry the parts over), apart from the page image's bytes (image: an item record has none) at the binder and the item's document at the splitter.
  • Item-unit components (ParagraphBuilder(unit="item"), DocumentComposer(unit="item")) read item records: one datatrove document per item, doc.metadata["item"] holding the item id and its page records in order (linecaster.core.item); they read and add the parts of the pages' transcriptions, the item DocumentComposer adds the item's document next to the record. Item writers (ItemDocumentWriter, ItemTextWriter) read the document and write it by each text's transcription strategy. RecipeStamper has unit any: before an item writer it stamps the pages of each item record.
  • A step without a contract (a plain datatrove step) passes pages and touches no part.
Component Reads Adds Replaces, removes LineAssigner lines, regions line_regions regions, reading_order, lines HierarchyDetector regions, lines hierarchy regions, lines ParagraphBuilder regions, lines paragraphs paragraphs (made anew where they exist) DocumentComposer regions, lines (and paragraphs when there are) document (rendered, not stored; no annotator) Tagger regions, lines (the model tagger: image and its targets, regions or lines) tags ImageFetcher metadata image ImageConverter metadata metadata (with keep_bytes also image; without it removes image) TranscriptionConverter metadata, transcription_file (with source="media") <transcription>:* RecipeStamper

items.title: Component shapes
items.text:
• Per-unit transform (shape = "unit"): process_page(doc, page) -> page | None; PageComponent owns the loop and the stats. In-process model components have this shape.
  • Stream transform (shape = "stream"): overrides run(data) and yields each page when it is done, possibly out of order (served model components, PageRecognizer, RegionRecognizer). It reports what happens to each page inside it with notify(doc, event): prepare when a request is built, done when its result came back. The served model components share one streaming loop (ModelComponent): a component names its requests (_rows: one per page, one per region for RegionRecognizer), builds and parses each (_request, _parse) and says which pages a finished one completes (_done).
  • Only readers and writers see rank, world_size and files (a test walks every component class, with no exceptions): a component that rejects a page records why on the page, and the RejectWriter names the task's file.

items.title: Backends
items.text:
A model component's backend (linecaster.backends) says where its engine runs:

  • InProcess("pkg:Class", **options) (or InProcess.from_preset(ref); a model component given a preset ref, LayoutDetector("single-region"), builds one): the engine loads in the worker;
  • Served(endpoint, model=name, ...): linecaster serve (or a server speaking its routes) hosts it, reached through saturate on /v1/linecaster/{step}; warm_up() refuses a server whose /health names another transcription format than linecaster.page/4, or none;
  • Chat(preset, endpoint=None, served_name=None, max_window=32, initial_window=4, read_timeout=600.0, api_key=None, headers=None, prefer="page"): a chat preset's VLM behind an OpenAI-compatible server (vLLM, SGLang, a hosted endpoint) on /v1/chat/completions; preset is a preset ref, a model's Hugging Face id (its preset with unit prefer) or a configured adapter (chat_model); without an endpoint, the task's VLMServer on port 8000. PageRecognizer(backend) and RegionRecognizer(backend, labels=..., pad=None) (pad: the adapter's region_pad, else 8) take it (or a chat preset's ref). Chat(..., overrides={...}) sets the chat engine's options over the preset's settings (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, repair_max_tokens, repair_temperature, repetition_detection; --set recognition.<option>=<value> in pipelines/transcribe_vlm.py, and --no-repetition-detection there to turn the last off: it is on by default where the preset's vLLM takes it); the ones that differ from the preset's are recorded with the adapter (overrides) and count in pipeline_sha256. With repair_max_tokens set, PageRecognizer runs the repair passes: a page whose completion stopped at max_tokens waits while its repair requests go into the same window, one per cap while each stops at its cap, and leaves the component with every pass recorded as a raw output (pass, kept: the one its annotations were parsed from); PageRecognizer(..., repair_only=True) sends only the repair requests, for page records read with PageRecordReader (--pages ... --repair-only). The streaming loop of ModelComponent offers this to every served component: a finished request may ask for a second one (_second_request), whose response comes back with it (_second_done), and that one for another (_next_request). PageRecognizer also takes a page engine's InProcess or Served backend (or its preset's ref): a stream transform served, a per-unit transform in-process; it reads the page image and adds text and what the preset produces. A page engine's endpoint option (where its service is) is operational.

The built-in engines (layout.single-region.v1, the rule-based steps' and the taggers) run in the pipeline's process only: runtime.run.engines keeps a preset of one in-process when the other models are served, and linecaster serve refuses them.

The Tagger (linecaster.components.tagging) runs a tagging engine on every page, by preset or engine spec like the rule components (Tagger("geometry-tags"), Tagger(InProcess("linecaster.engines:ChatTaggingEngine", schemes=["degraded"], panel=[...])), options over either), and adds tags: classifications in property schemes (data model). It decodes the page image only for an engine that reads it (the model tagger, a client of chat servers that the run provides), and passes the page's id, which review items name. Stats: tagged, undecided.

items.title: The builder
items.text:
plan = build(components, tasks=8, until=None, after=None, taps={"LineAssigner": "OUT/taps/lines"},
             run_folder="OUT", recipe=("squiddle", "sha256:..."))
plan.check()          # PipelineConfigError listing every problem
plan.stages           # [Stage(name, tasks, components, pipeline)]: one datatrove pipeline each, run in order
plan.graph            # nodes (components; composites expanded, their group kept), edges (part -> the component reading it)
plan.mermaid()        # the graph as a Mermaid flowchart: stages and composites as subgraphs
plan.describe()       # stages with each component's contract, the edges, the problems

Checks, all collected: a stage starts with a reader; every part a component reads is added earlier in its stage (or by the stage's reader) and not removed since (removes, even after a reader that provides anything); a part is added by one component only, unless a later component declares it in replaces; units fit (a page component cannot follow an item stream, an item component needs a binder before it); the parts carry across a binder and a splitter (apart from image and the item's document); server components go last; a served model component whose endpoint is a server component of its stage (same loopback port) finds its model in that server's list; the alternatives of a group add the same parts, sit next to each other, each with a condition, OTHERWISE last; names given to until, after and taps fit exactly one component.

Order is the given one; the builder checks it and does not reorder. It inserts a TranscriptionConverter (into ocr_original) right after a component that adds transcription_file when no later component reads it, the RecipeStamper before the first writer when the run follows a recipe, a RejectWriter into <run_folder>/rejects before the first writer (or binder) when there is a run folder and the pipeline has none, and moves the server components at the end into the stage of the model components when it cuts. build(..., max_page_errors=SHARE) sets every page component's error budget.

Branches: branch(component, when=Condition, group=None) gives a component a condition, a picklable predicate on the page record with a describe() (MetadataEquals(key, value), OTHERWISE). The component processes the pages the condition accepts; the others pass unchanged. Components with the same group are alternatives: each page goes through the first one whose condition accepts it. A per-unit component gets its pages one by one; any other component one stream of them, the pages it does not take passed on as it yields.

Composites: Composite(name, components, contract=None) expands into its components (nested composites too); its outward contract is derived (what its components read that none of them adds, what they add and replace) unless given. ModularTranscriber(lines, recognition, layout, formulas_separately=False, transcription="ocr_new") is layout ("single-region": the page as one region) → lines → line assignment → line recognition; each step a component, a backend or a preset.

Stages: with tasks > 1, the first binder (a component whose stream changes from pages to items) cuts the pipeline, unless the reader already gives each task whole items (ManifestReader, PageRecordReader(item_shards= True)). The first stage writes its page records in item shards into <run_folder>/pages/ (the pipeline's own PageJsonlWriter there, now with item_shards=N, N = tasks unless it set its own); the second starts with PageRecordReader(item_shards=True, fetch_images=False) declaring the parts the first stage added, runs the binder and what follows, as N tasks. A ItemSplitter after the binder needs no cut of its own: the items are whole in the task, so its pages are too. One stage logs to OUT/logs/, two to OUT/logs/pages/ and OUT/logs/items/; the run record lists the stages. Each stage gets its own executor, and the later one depends= on the earlier one:

--on Executors Stages local LocalPipelineExecutor the second starts when the first is complete ray RayGPUExecutor for stages with servers, RayExecutor for the item stage and pipelines without engines (CPUs only) the same, through depends= hf-jobs JobsExecutor (datatrove's JobsPipelineExecutor with JSON-lines logs; GPUJobsExecutor for multi-GPU flavors on stages with servers) consecutive launches: the second launches when the first's Jobs are complete; both on --flavor

Partial runs (components named by their datatrove name, their class name, or a composite's name for its last component):

  • until=BLOCK (--until): the components up to and including BLOCK, then a PageJsonlWriter into <run_folder>/pages (and the server components);
  • after=BLOCK (--after, with --pages DIR): the pipeline's PageRecordReader, then the components after BLOCK; the reader declares the parts the components up to BLOCK add;
  • taps={BLOCK: DIR} (--tap-after BLOCK DIR, repeatable): a Tap observer writes every page record as it leaves BLOCK into DIR/<rank>.jsonl.gz.

In this process: run_pages(components, docs) checks the components and runs them on docs (datatrove documents) as task 0 of 1, without an executor (a leading reader reads its own input after them); run_plan(plan) runs a plan's stages that way. A pipeline script's --page IMAGE OUT runs its pipeline on one image like that, and linecaster page IMAGE OUT [--recipe R | --pipeline ID] [pipeline options] finds the script (the recipe's pipeline, else transcribe_modular.v1) and runs it so.

--dry-run prints the plan (describe() under plan, with the run record) and the Mermaid graph, and fails like a run would when there are problems; a run with problems exits with code 2 before it writes anything.

items.title: Observers
items.text:
linecaster.core.observers.Observer has on_task_start(rank, world_size), on_warm_up(component, seconds), on_enter(component, doc), on_exit(component, doc, error=None), on_unit(component, doc, event, **attributes) (from stream components' notify: prepare and request in saturate's prepare threads, request with a carrier dict for the trace context, done with error, tokens and finish_reason; region for a request per region), on_task_event(block, event, start_ns, end_ns, **attributes) (from Component.report: a reader's file, a writer's flush), on_leave(doc) (a page leaves the stage's last component), on_task_end(error=None) (also when the task fails) and environment() (variables for a server a component starts in the task). When a stage has observers (build(..., observers=[...]), taps, tracing), the builder puts a Boundary after every component: the boundary between component i and i + 1 calls on_exit(i) and on_enter(i + 1) for each page, so a component's time per page includes waiting in a served window; error is the entry the component added to doc.metadata["errors"]. Boundaries are plain callables, not datatrove steps, so they add no stats; a stage without observers has none.

Every stage with a run folder (or an OTLP endpoint) is traced: the builder adds a linecaster.tracing.Tracing observer (build(..., trace_share=SHARE), --trace-share; tracing).

items.title: Warm-up
items.text: Every component has warm_up() (idempotent): engines load there (InProcess.warm_up()), servers start there (EngineServer, VLMServer), a served backend reads its secrets there; components with nothing to load keep the no-op. A component's __call__, which datatrove's executors call, warms it up before its run starts: components warm up as the stream reaches them, the last one first (the servers before the components that call them). The time is the component's own stat, warm_up_seconds (per task), and goes to the observers (on_warm_up(component, seconds)); a page's measured seconds never include loading. An error in a warm-up fails the task (a server that does not start: a ServerError).

items.title: Failures
items.text:
• Per page. An exception in a per-unit transform's process_page (other than a PipelineConfigError, CatalogError or ServerError, which fail the task) becomes an entry in the page's doc.metadata["errors"]: {"component": class, "step": a model component's step, "preset": its id or null, "type": the exception's class, "error": the message}; a failed request of a served component is the same with type ServerError; checks (PageValidator, ImageConverter) add field and raw_value. The page goes on as it was.
  • Later model components pass it by (skip_on_error, the default for model components; stat skipped_after_error), at once: in-process the page leaves the component before the next one enters, served it is put straight onto the component's results (it never waits for the window, nor for the end of the input).
  • Rejects. The RejectWriter writes every page that carries errors to OUT/rejects/<rank>.jsonl, one line per error (key, field, error, raw_value, and the entry's component, step, preset, type), and passes it on: the page records keep failed pages with their errors, so a later pipeline reading them passes them by too. PageFileWriter(skip_failed=True) writes no per-page files for them (the modular pipeline's --files), so a file is never what the components before the failure made of a page.
  • The error budget. A component may fail on max_page_errors of a task's pages (--max-page-errors, default 0.01), judged from the 100th page on: from then, more errors than share × pages fail the task with a PageError (with the default: two failures in the first 100 pages, three in 300). Fewer pages are too few to judge. datatrove reruns a failed task whole.
  • Page images (linecaster.images.pixels). The model components give engines plain 8-bit RGB pixels (Pillow's convert("RGB") of the file: no ICC profile applied, no EXIF orientation), decoded once per page and process: the components after the first that needs a page's image use the same read-only array (stats image_decoded, image_shared). --image-decode (ModelComponent.image_decode, set by the builder) says how: auto (the default) decodes JPEG, JPEG 2000 and TIFF in 8-bit gray or RGB on an NVIDIA GPU where the machine has one and linecaster[nvimgcodec] is installed, the worker's GPU, everything else with Pillow; cpu always with Pillow; gpu like auto, but a machine without a GPU is an error. A served component sends its choice with the image, and linecaster serve decodes there; a chat adapter builds its request from the same pixels. A GPU and Pillow round a lossy image's pixels differently, so a step records its decoder (measurement decoder); an image a GPU refuses, or a GPU that fails, is decoded with Pillow (stats gpu_decoded, cpu_decoded, gpu_decode_refused, gpu_decode_errors). The option is operational: it is not part of pipeline_sha256, since auto depends on the machine anyway.
  • Errors (linecaster.errors): library code raises PipelineConfigError (a pipeline, option or input that cannot work; problems lists them), CatalogError, PageError(page_id, component) and ServerError, all LinecasterErrors, never SystemExit; the linecaster command and a pipeline script's main turn them into exit codes (2: nothing was launched).

items.title: The run record
items.text:
OUT/run.yaml (schema linecaster.run-record/2, the pydantic model linecaster.execution.record.RunRecord, JSON Schema catalog/schemas/run-record-2.json) records the script, the recipe, the command line, the options, where it ran and the software, and:

  • pipeline: per stage its name, tasks and components in order, each component as its to_dict() (below) with its contract, composite, group and condition;
  • pipeline_sha256: the hash of the pipeline's functional parameters.

to_dict() gives a component as it was built: {"component": class name, "class": "module:Class", "params": {...}}, every constructor parameter with the value it was given or its default (**kwargs flattened), JSON-compatible: backends as {"backend": "in-process", "engine", "options", "preset", "preset_sha256"}, {"backend": "served", "endpoint", "model", "max_window", ..., "preset", "engine"} or {"backend": "chat", "adapter", "preset", "preset_sha256", "model", "revision", "served_name", "endpoint", "max_window", ...} (a chat adapter's dict plus where its server is), nested components as their dicts, secrets as {"env": NAME}, folders as paths, callables as module:name. A component keeps the arguments it was constructed with; live_params names those the builder may change afterwards (a page record reader's provides). A composite's dict is its group: its parameters and its components' dicts.

Functional and operational parameters. A parameter is functional when changing it can change what a run writes for a page or an item (its page records, files and texts) or how they are partitioned (item_shards); it is operational when it only changes where things are read and written, how the work is spread and paced, or how a server is reached. pipeline_sha256 covers the functional ones (provenance.functional_pipeline):

Operational (left out) Why folders and file names: data_folder, output_folder, output_filename, image_folder, manifest_folder, ocr_folder, folder, suffix, bucket_by_item, prefix where things are which input files a task reads and how: paths_file, glob_pattern, recursive, limit, skip, shuffle_files, batch_size (a reader's), http (rate limits, the IIIF format asked for), uri_map, progress bars the pages themselves are recorded per page servers and clients: port, host, python, script, vllm, outside_venv, boot_timeout, max_queue, prepare_workers, gpu_memory_utilization, extra_args; an in-process engine's endpoint and timeout (ENGINE_OPERATIONAL: where its service is); a served backend's endpoint, model (the name it is hosted under, unless nothing else names its engine), max_window, initial_window, read_timeout, api_key, headers; a chat backend's served_name and the same (it counts by its adapter, preset and hash, model and revision) how a server is started and reached name (datatrove's display name), compression, max_file_size, ImageConverter.keep_bytes, .skip_existing, .window, .initial_window, .max_window, ImageFolderReader.read_images presentation, file handling, memory, how many pages are in flight server components (EngineServer, VLMServer, VendorServer) as a whole their models count through the components they serve the backend (in-process or served) a model component counts by its engine, the engine's options and the preset with its hash, wherever it runs

Everything else is functional: component classes and their order, transcription names, engine options, presets and their hashes, the recipe stamp, conditions and groups, writers' formats, texts and strategies, item_shards. The base list is OPERATIONAL in linecaster.core.component; a component class adds its own in operational. A parameter added to a released component with a default that keeps the old behavior is left out while it has that default (unhashed_defaults, e.g. PageRecognizer's repair_only), so the pipelines that do not use it keep their hash. So a resumed run, a run on another executor or backend, or into another folder has the same hash; another preset, option or component has another.

Resume. A run into an OUT that holds a run record is checked against its newest record (run.yaml, or a later run-<time>.yaml): another pipeline_sha256 is refused with a PipelineConfigError (finished tasks would be skipped and the folder would mix two pipelines' outputs) unless --new-pipeline (the new record is written next to the earlier one and is the one the next resume is checked against); another --tasks is always refused (each task would read other input), and so is another sample (the record's sample.selected.sha256, samples). The same hash, tasks and sample: a resume, as datatrove's completion markers make it. --dry-run reports the same problems.

Describe mode. linecaster.execution.run.describe(template, argv) builds a pipeline template's plan in the current process without its engines: its options parsed, presets resolved without checking that their engines are installed, nothing loaded or started. describe_recipe(ref) describes a recipe that way (the template of the recipe's pipeline id, linecaster.templates.template(id), with --recipe REF and placeholder folders): what linecaster catalog index records as the recipe's pipeline_sha256 and verify compares (catalog).

items.title: Samples
items.text:
A run reads a sample of its input with a sample rule: --sample N (at most N pages in all), --sample-per-item K (at most K pages of each item), --sample-items M (at most M items), --sample-seed S (default 0); any of the first three alone or together. The sample is chosen by the ids of the input's listing alone, before any image is read or fetched, and is the same whatever --tasks, executor or machine: an evaluation then scores every system on the same pages, and others can recompute them from the list of ids without linecaster.

The rule (linecaster.data.sample, linecaster.sample/1), with H(s) the first 8 bytes of sha256(s) (UTF-8) as an unsigned big-endian integer:

  1. The listing is the input's distinct (item_id, page_id) pairs; a page without item has the item id "". An id with a tab is an error.
  2. Items are ordered by (H(f"{seed}\t{item_id}"), item_id) (the item rank), and only the first M are kept. An item without pages takes no rank.
  3. Within an item, pages are ordered by (H(f"{seed}\t{item_id}\t{page_id}"), page_id) (the page rank), and only the first K are kept; an item with fewer pages gives them all.
  4. The pages, in the order (item rank, page rank), are cut after the first N.

The page hash includes the item, so items whose pages are named alike (0001.png in every item folder) do not all give the same positions. A rank depends only on its ids and the seed: an item added to the input moves no other item's pages, and a sample of N is the first N pages of a sample of 2N. With K the first N pages come from about N/K items. In Python:

import hashlib

def h(*ids):
    return int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256("\t".join(map(str, ids)).encode()).digest()[:8], "big")

def sample(pairs, seed=0, n=None, k=None, m=None):
    items = {}
    for i, p in dict.fromkeys(pairs): items.setdefault(i, []).append(p)
    order = sorted(items, key=lambda i: (h(seed, i), i))[:m]
    return [(i, p) for i in order for p in sorted(items[i], key=lambda p: (h(seed, i, p), p))[:k]][:n]

The first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 sort as H does, so SQL can order by them. A stratum is a separate run over a filtered input.

Per input (the readers' sample, linecaster.components.readers.sampling):

Input Ids Read before the sample The tasks IMAGES (--item-from-parent for items) the parent folder, the file name without extension the file listing the sample's files in turn --parquet (--item-key for items) --id-key, or <item>_<0001> from --item-key and --sequence-key the id columns only the sample's rows in equal shards (by item with task_per_item); a row's image is read with the other sample rows of its row group --manifests the item id of each entry, <item>_<0001> for its pages the item ids; then the manifests of the items in rank order, as far as the rule reaches (every one with --sample-per-item alone) the sample's items as the entries would be; only their sample pages' images are requested --pages page.item_id, id every record (no image) their files as without a sample, passing on the sample's records alone

--sample-per-item and --sample-items need items. An id listed twice is read once (its first entry), counted in the record's duplicates. With --manifests the manifests the sample reads are saved to OUT/manifests/ with an index (sample.jsonl: item id, entry, the URL it was read from, the copy's file, its pages); the tasks read those copies instead of fetching them again, and so does a resume when it computes the sample again. A manifest that cannot be read, or a IIIF Collection entry, stops the launch: the sample would depend on it. --max-pages and a sample exclude each other; --limit and --skip still count per task, over the task's share.

The launch computes the sample once, before the tasks (linecaster.execution.run.sampled); it travels with the pickled pipeline, and each task takes its share. It is recorded in the run record's sample section:

Field Holds rule, hash linecaster.sample/1 and the hashes in words pages, items, per_item, seed N, M, K and S listing scope (pages, or items for manifests, whose pages are known once read), items, pages, duplicates, manifests_read, sha256: of the distinct sorted lines item_id<TAB>page_id (for manifests item_id), each with a newline selected items, pages, sha256: of the sample's lines item_id<TAB>page_id in sample order, each with a newline file sample.parquet

OUT/sample.parquet (linecaster.execution.sample) holds one row per sample page in sample order: rank (1-based: a sample of N is rank <= N), item_id, page_id, item_rank, page_rank, item_hash, page_hash (unsigned 64 bit) and item_pages (the item's pages in the listing), with the record's section in the file's metadata (linecaster.sample). The same sample gives the same rows and metadata, and with the same pyarrow the same bytes; selected.sha256 compares samples across versions. linecaster sample [IMAGES] OUT with the input and sample options writes it without a run (with --manifests, the manifests too), as a run with the same options would. A sample's options are operational parameters (the pipeline's hash leaves them out); a resume with another sample is refused.

items.title: Tasks, workers and rate limits
items.text:
--tasks and --workers are chosen when the command line leaves them open (linecaster.execution.run.allocate):

Pipeline --tasks --workers with engines 1 every task without engines, every rate-limited host through proxies (--proxies, an HTTP policy's proxies: {file}), local or Ray (--on hf-jobs: as below) the reader's auto_tasks (from the input), else 1 sharing them fairly (proxies: {per_worker: share}, the default): one per available proxy, at most one per CPU; with per_worker 1 or N: one per available proxy divided by N (ceil(available / N)), not capped by the CPUs; either way at most the tasks and, with OUT on object storage, at most 64 (OBJECT_STORAGE_WORKERS) without engines, with --rate-limit (a host with rate limits and no proxies) the reader's auto_tasks, else 1 1 without engines, without --rate-limit the reader's auto_tasks, else 1 one per CPU, at most the tasks

The available proxies are counted once at launch from one listing of the broker (linecaster.execution.run.available_proxies): those in the file, less those with a live block or broken mark for the run's hosts (any host when the hosts are not named in an HTTP policy) and those leased by live workers of other runs (the run's own earlier leases count as available); on a first launch, without a broker yet, all of them. Sharing the proxies fairly, a few workers use them all, so their count stops at the CPUs; with one proxy per worker (or up to N) using them all takes a worker per proxy (per N), and the workers mostly wait on the network, so their count is not capped by the CPUs. With OUT on object storage (any fsspec protocol but a local one: s3://, gs://, hf://, az://, ...) the count stops at linecaster.execution.run.OBJECT_STORAGE_WORKERS (64) in both modes: in one setup, 250 workers writing to S3-compatible object storage hung in their listings of OUT/images and fetched less than 64 did, which ran cleanly; an observation from that setup, not a guarantee for others. The run states the count and why (linecaster.execution.run.workers_note, e.g. 250 proxies available, OUT on object storage → 64 workers, a fair share each, or 250 proxies available → 250 workers, 1 proxy each). --workers overrides it (each worker is a process with its own memory).

auto_tasks is about 1,000 pages per task for ImageParquetReader and about 5 items per task for ManifestReader (linecaster.components.readers.tables.PAGES_PER_TASK, ITEMS_PER_TASK), so a resume repeats little. The harvest (pipelines/harvest.py) asks its reader for one item per task (task_per_item): the tasks divide the items, an item's rows wherever they are in the table (tables.item_runs), so every item is whole in its task and a task that fails costs one item. With --reuse (off by default: on some object storage a listing is slow even for an empty folder, and only the items a stopped launch was in, or with --retry-failed the finished items with failed pages, have anything to reuse) its reader also gets reuse_folder (OUT/images): when it reaches an item it lists the item's folder once (an fsspec listing) and reads a page whose image file is already there from the storage instead of fetching it from the source (linecaster.components.readers.existing); only pages of interrupted items (and of the items --retry-failed runs again, whose failed pages alone are then fetched) are read back, so egress stays small. The reader waits at most LISTING_TIMEOUT (60 s) for a listing (on object storage fsspec cancels it then on its IO loop): one that times out or fails is a warning and a stat (reuse_listing_timeouts, reuse_listing_errors), and the item's pages are fetched again, their files overwritten. Such a record is complete and says image.extra.reused; the console counts it as done but not in the rate. On a restart the console's size starts with the finished tasks' media_size from datatrove's stats files (linecaster.execution.local.size_before, read in the background). Parquet tables are divided over the tasks by rows in equal shards, not by files, so a table never needs splitting for a task count. --max-pages N (--parquet, IMAGES; the readers' max_pages) reads the input as if it ended after its first N pages, in the same automatic tasks: a smoke test of the real setup. --limit counts per task, as in datatrove. The same pages for every setup and input order: a sample.

--rate-limit holds per worker: each worker process has one fetcher with its limits (HTTPFetcher.shared), so a server sees the workers running at once times the limits; the run states it before it starts (linecaster.execution.run.rate_note, e.g. rate limits per worker: 150/60, 3/1 · 1 worker → up to 150/min at a server). One worker keeps any rate limit busy: a reader's requests ahead grow while none waits for the limits (linecaster.net.http.prefetched, at most MAX_AHEAD), and the fetcher, with its limits and the window it has grown to, is shared by the tasks a worker runs one after the other (HTTPFetcher.shared). With --proxies the limits hold per proxy instead (below), and the run states that (rate limits per proxy: 150/60 · 100 proxies → up to 15,000/min at a server; with fewer workers than proxies · 10 of 100 proxies in use (1 proxy per worker)).

Proxies. --proxies FILE sends the http(s) requests through a list of proxies, shared by the workers through the broker (--broker PATH, any fsspec folder, default OUT/logs/broker; runs pointed at one path share the proxies and their blocks too). Each proxy has one worker at a time, the one that holds its lease, and each worker holds a fair share of them (linecaster.net.proxies.ProxyPool, per_worker: share, the default): of the proxies not blocked for the host, divided by the live workers, claimed at most 2 at a time and grown by rebalancing, which also gives back what is beyond it when another worker joins. An HTTP policy's proxies: {per_worker: ...} (per host or at the root; hosts that share a list share the setting) gives a worker one proxy instead (1: it claims a free one usable for the host and, when that one is blocked or broken, releases it and claims another at once), or up to N, claimed one by one; with output on local disk or a short list, one per worker and a worker per proxy is the simplest way to use them all. The host's rate limits hold per proxy, so per IP, as servers count them: the owner spaces the requests through a proxy to a host by the strictest limit, and each request goes through the owned proxy whose turn comes first. A proxy is left out when the failure is its own (http). A block (a status in the host's block_on, 429 by default, and with html there an HTML page where another format was expected) is a mark in the broker for that host, until its Retry-After, else for 60 s, doubling on each repeat up to the host's block_ttl (an hour by default): the owner stops using the proxy there at once, releases it once it is blocked for every host it uses, and whoever claims it later sees the mark, so no worker sends a request into another's block, and a restarted run none into a block it found before. A broken proxy (a proxy error, no connection to it, broken_after failures in a row, 3 by default) is marked for every host, first for broken_ttl (5 minutes), doubling up to block_ttl. A block does not count as an attempt and the request goes on through another proxy at once, so max_retries (retries after the first attempt) counts only the attempts that reached the server and failed there; a component does not count toward the breaker either. A timeout is mostly a slow server: it is retried and leaves the proxy in. When none of a worker's proxies is usable for a host and none is free to claim, its requests to the host pause until a block ends or another worker gives a proxy back (one warning when the pause starts, one when it ends; the wait is in the fetch record's pause_seconds); once the waits since the host's last successful response would pass its max_pause (6 hours; http) the run stops (StopRequests) and says when the first proxy returns. An HTTP policy can set proxies: {block_ttl: 72h, broken_after: 1} and further statuses that block at the host (block_on: [429, 403], block_on: [429, html]). The console shows the proxies the worker holds, those blocked and those free. On Ray each task is a process of its own; the next task on a machine takes over the worker slot the last one handed over, and with it its proxies. The file holds one proxy per line, a URL or host:port[:user:pass] as Webshare lists them; the run record keeps its name, logs show proxies without credentials (linecaster.net.http.redact), and the broker names them by a hash of host and port.

Failures. Each fetcher has a breaker (linecaster.net.http.Breaker): when most attempts of the last minute got a server error (5xx, Cloudflare's 520-524 among them), its requests pause, a probe goes out now and then (waits doubling from one to ten minutes), and the first answer that is not a server error lets them go on; the pages wait instead of failing. A single server error is retried (with a proxy list without counting against the proxy it came through). A block on a direct connection (a status in the host's block_on, 429 by default) pauses the worker that got it (linecaster.net.http.Pause): its requests to that host wait until the response's Retry-After has passed (seconds or an HTTP-date; without one a minute, doubling while components keep coming), then the request that got it is tried again, without using up one of its retries; blocks for requests already in flight extend the pause, never shorten it. The pages wait instead of failing, and the requests to other hosts and other workers go on. The log says when a pause starts (host, status, how long, until when) and when the requests go on, and a page's fetch record has the time paused (pause_seconds). A worker that would pause more than the host's max_pause (6 hours) since its last successful response stops the run: the worker waits, or stops when the wait would be too long (http, one count for both paths). Through proxies a block leaves that proxy out at the host instead (above). An HTML page where an image, XML or JSON was expected is a failed attempt, retried like a server error, unless the host's policy makes it a block or a stop (http). A local task that fails is logged and the others go on (LocalExecutor); it runs again on the next launch. An error that is not the pages' (NOT_THE_PAGES) or FAILED_IN_A_ROW failed tasks in a row in one worker stop the run. --retry-failed runs the finished tasks that left rejects again; kill -USR1 <pid> dumps every thread's stack. On Ray (linecaster.execution.ray.RayExecutor) the same error stops the run through a marker in the logging folder (stopped.json): every task after it ends before its pipeline starts, so none sends a request into the component that stopped the first, and the launch fails with that task's error; a launch that left tasks unfinished fails too, so the Ray job does not end as succeeded. A new launch removes the marker. Before it submits a task, a Ray launch checks that a live node has what a task reserves (--cpus-per-task; --mem-per-task-gb, else --mem-per-cpu-gb per CPU; one GPU for a stage with models) and stops with a PipelineConfigError if none has, where Ray would keep the tasks waiting without an error; --no-fit-check leaves the check out, for a cluster that adds nodes on demand. A task sizes the native thread pools to the CPUs it may use (linecaster.execution.cpus: its Ray CPUs, else the cgroup's CPU quota), and so do the worker counts a launch derives "one per CPU".

Resources. pipelines/harvest.py --items TABLE --item-key COL fetches items' remote files other than page images (ResourceReader): from URL templates per kind (--resource marcxml=https://catalog.example.org/{item}/marcxml) or a table with one row per resource (--url-key, --kind-key, --name-key). Each is checked (XML, JSON or an image must parse, a DjVu file must start with its signature; an HTML page where another format was expected is retried, and a resource that fails with it counts toward the breaker) and kept as a raw copy, OUT/<kind>/<item>/<name>.<ext> (ResourceFilesWriter), the reference later stages link to, with its fetch record in OUT/resources/<rank>.jsonl.gz (ResourceRecordWriter: source and final URL, status, type, size, sha256, ETag, Last-Modified, time). One item per task, --max-items for a smoke test, copies already there read back. --http-policy FILE gives the run's requests their settings from one YAML file (linecaster.net.policy, http): for every host at the root, and under hosts: an entry for each host that differs, whose fields replace the root's; the run's own options go between the two. The settings: rate limits (per proxy through proxies), retries (max_retries), deadline, User-Agent, what blocks (block_on, default [429]; with html an HTML page where another format was expected) and what stops the run without a retry (stop_on: statuses and html; something in both block_on, or its default, and stop_on is refused, so block_on: [] with stop_on: [429] stops on a 429), max_pause, direct, the proxy path's own section (proxies: {file, per_worker, block_ttl, broken_after, broken_ttl}) and the broker (root only). The run states the rules that hold per host before it starts. For every input fetched over http(s): --items, --parquet with http(s) image URLs, --manifests (the manifests, their images and OCR files) and --pages (the images it fetches again); with rate limits in the file for a host without proxies a run keeps one worker, with proxies for every rate-limited host its workers follow the available proxies (above).

The default User-Agent is datatrove's, HF-Research/1.0 (linecaster.net.http.USER_AGENT), deliberately: datatrove is integral to linecaster, and its media fetcher (HTTPFetchReader) sends the same, so a run that fetches through both presents itself as one client to every host. --user-agent or an HTTP policy's user_agent sets another.

items.title: The console
items.text: A local run (--on local, linecaster.execution.local.LocalExecutor) shows on the terminal: one line naming the pipeline (its components, without the builder's boundaries; pages, tasks and workers; what an earlier launch finished), a live progress line (pages done of the total, rate over the last five minutes, size, failed pages, the task, the time left) pinned to the terminal's top row, with everything else scrolling below it (a scroll region, Pinned), a line per finished task and a summary, in human units (linecaster.execution.console). The Progress observer, which the runtime puts on every stage, counts the pages that leave the pipeline; with several workers each worker process reports its counts to the console about every second. Off a terminal the progress is a log line every 30 s instead. datatrove's own console output (its pipeline listing and stats component per task, the merged stats) goes only to the task logs (OUT/logs/logs/task_<rank>.log, in its full line format) and the stats files, which keep it whole. A launch lists the completion markers once instead of looking them up task by task.

items.title: Secrets
items.text: linecaster.secrets.EnvVar("NAME") names an environment variable; the value is read in the task (resolve()), never stored: an EnvVar pickles by name, to_dict() writes {"env": "NAME"}. Served(endpoint, model, api_key=EnvVar("NAME"), headers={"X-Team": "ocr", "X-Token": EnvVar("TOKEN")}) (and Chat(preset, endpoint, api_key=..., headers=...) alike) sends Authorization: Bearer <key> and the headers with every request through saturate's AdaptiveClient(headers=...); a key given as text is refused. A missing variable fails the component's warm-up.

items.title: Pipeline templates
items.text:
A pipeline script's code is a pipeline template in linecaster.templates (harvest, convert, transcribe_modular, transcribe_vlm, transcribe_page, bind, import_transcriptions, score): its docstring (the help text), options(ap), models(a), pipeline(a, script), PIPELINE and, where recipes fill it, SLOTS. linecaster.templates.templates() lists them by pipeline id and template(id) finds one; importing one imports no engine. The script in pipelines/ is its PEP 723 block, a docstring and the call that runs the template:

from linecaster.templates import transcribe_modular as template
from linecaster.execution import run

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run.main(__file__, template.__doc__, template.options, template.models, template.pipeline, template.PIPELINE,
             template.SLOTS)

A downstream project's script runs a shape the same way, in its own environment (the engine packages its slots need), and may lay its own defaults over the shape's options: an options that calls the shape's and then ap.set_defaults(...) (--recipe too, which run adds before the script's options), and a pipeline that fills a default depending on other options before it calls the shape's. Its run records name its script; its pipeline_sha256 is the shape's for the same options.

items.title: Importing ground truth
items.text: pipelines/import_transcriptions.py (import_transcriptions.v1) reads a source's documents into page records with one importer (step import, slot import): a Parquet table's column holding each document (--data-key: a wiki page's wikitext), a column naming a file (--uri-key), or the file delivered with the page; --context-key columns are the document's context, record, revision and dataset its source's fields. Its pages are named, not read (ImageParquetReader(read_images=False), or no --image-key): importing needs no image. Its page records are what linecaster score reads as a ground truth, and what a dataset is assembled from.

items.title: The item stage
items.text:
The item-level steps follow a ItemAssembler; the usual shape (pipelines/bind.py, and --item-texts of pipelines/transcribe_modular.py):

texts = ("literal:txt", "latin-historic+unicode-marks+flow:md")   # --text, repeatable
[PageRecordReader(pages, fetch_images=False, item_shards=True),
 ItemAssembler(),                                                  # page records -> item records
 ParagraphBuilder("unicode-paragraphs", unit="item"),        # paragraphs continued across page breaks
 DocumentComposer("linked-document", unit="item"),             # the item's document, literal
 ItemDocumentWriter(f"{out}/documents", texts=texts),     # documents/<strategy>/<item>.<ext>
 ItemTextWriter(f"{out}/texts", texts=texts)]             # texts/<strategy>.<format>/<rank>.jsonl.gz (bind: --jsonl)

A text is the item's document written by a transcription strategy in a format (<strategy>:<format>: literal or a catalog strategy, normalizations joined by + too; md, txt, html, json); nothing is normalized unless a text names a strategy, and bind writes only the literal document as JSON unless --text names others. A JSON Lines row holds id (the item), text, spec, strategy, strategy_sha256, normalizations, format, page_ids, pages and token_count with a token counter. The page files (PageFileWriter) take one strategy too (--strategy, default literal).

A ItemSplitter after the item-level components passes each item's pages on as pages (e.g. to a PageJsonlWriter), with the paragraphs of the item recomposition.

items.title: Page records
items.text: Stored page records are rows {"schema": "linecaster.page/6", "id", "text", "page", "errors"} (PageJsonlWriter, PageParquetWriter; PAGE_SCHEMA in linecaster.data.page): page is the page record of the data model, its annotation sets with their annotators, raw outputs and annotations. Renderings (the DocumentComposer's document, the files, the texts) are not part of it. PageRecordReader brings older rows to today's format (UPGRADES, keyed by the row's schema, one version at a time): a linecaster.page/4 row through page_4_to_5 (the derived text dropped, data model); a linecaster.page/2 row through linecaster.data.upgrade.page_2_to_3 (field by field in the data model); a linecaster.page/1 row, whose transcriptions name their steps model, to page/2 first; a row without schema (the oldest format) names its transcription ocr, read as ocr_new; a .../pages folder without records is read from its sibling rows/ (the folder's earlier name).

items.title: Rendering policy
items.text: The components that render (DocumentComposer, PageFileWriter, ItemDocumentWriter, ItemTextWriter) take policy, a catalog policy (id, default page-layers; catalog), which decides the layer of each region in the documents, files and texts they write (data model). pipelines/transcribe_modular.py and pipelines/bind.py set it with --policy; it is a functional parameter, so the run record names it and pipeline_sha256 covers it.

items.title: HF Jobs helpers
items.text:
A launch with --on hf-jobs names --namespace, the Hugging Face user or organization the Jobs run under and are billed to, and --commit, the linecaster commit the Jobs install (pushed). Neither has a default, and the namespace is not taken from the logged-in account, so the account a run spends is always the one its command line and run record name. --commit is required for linecaster's own scripts; a downstream project's script outside the linecaster checkout that takes linecaster from a git tag, branch or rev runs without it (jobs.needs_commit), since its Jobs install what its sources name.

linecaster.execution.jobs.dependencies(commit, script=None, engines=True) spells out what a Job installs from a pipeline script, linecaster's or a downstream project's, as Dependencies:

  • requirements: the script's dependencies with their sources as PEP 508 URLs (url as it is; git with its tag, branch or rev and its subdirectory, as git+URL@REF#subdirectory=DIR; a path into the linecaster checkout as GitHub's source archive of linecaster at commit, any other path an error), then every package reachable from them in the script's lock that comes from no index (the sources the packages declare themselves: the kraken fork at its locked commit, the OpenCV stub);
  • constraints: every package reachable from them that the lock takes from an index, at the lock's version (name==version; a package the lock holds at several versions with its resolution markers), so a Job resolves the versions of the lock; none for a script without a lock;
  • overrides: the script's [tool.uv] override-dependencies (a lock that resolves only with them, such as transcribe_page.py's pillow==12.3.0 over surya-ocr's pillow<11).

linecaster's ray extra is left out. engines=False keeps linecaster with its extras and the sources they need, and the constraints of what those reach; without a script it raises unless engines=False (linecaster alone).
